question: Let (G, .) and (H, *) be groups with identities e_G and e_H, and let phi: G -> H be a group homomorphism, meaning phi(x.y) = phi(x)*phi(y) for all x, y in G. Prove from the homomorphism property alone (without assuming phi is injective, surjective, or that G or H is finite) that phi(e_G) = e_H and that phi(g^{-1}) = phi(g)^{-1} for every g in G. State explicitly which group axioms (uniqueness of identity, uniqueness of inverses, cancellation) you invoke at each step, and explain why these two facts justify the standing claims that every representation phi satisfies phi(e) = 1_V and phi(g^{-1}) = phi(g)^{-1}.
reference_answer: For the identity: pick any g in G and write g = e_G . g, so phi(g) = phi(e_G . g) = phi(e_G) * phi(g). Thus phi(e_G) * phi(g) = phi(g) = e_H * phi(g). Right-multiplying both sides by phi(g)^{-1} in H (which exists because H is a group) and cancelling gives phi(e_G) = e_H; equivalently, phi(e_G) acts as a left identity on phi(g), and since the identity of H is unique, phi(e_G) = e_H. For the inverse: fix g in G. Then e_H = phi(e_G) = phi(g . g^{-1}) = phi(g) * phi(g^{-1}), and likewise e_H = phi(g^{-1} . g) = phi(g^{-1}) * phi(g). So phi(g^{-1}) is a two-sided inverse of phi(g) in H; because inverses in a group are unique, phi(g^{-1}) = phi(g)^{-1}. The only axioms used are the homomorphism identity, the group axioms e_G . g = g and g . g^{-1} = g^{-1} . g = e_G in G, existence of inverses in H (to cancel), and uniqueness of the identity and of inverses in H. Applied to a representation phi: G -> GL(V) with H = GL(V) and identity 1_V, these say precisely phi(e) = 1_V and phi(g^{-1}) = phi(g)^{-1}; in particular every phi(g) is automatically invertible with the stated inverse, so invertibility need not be postulated separately.

question: Let (phi, V) be a finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group G, and let <.|.> be any inner product on V. Define the averaged form <v|w>_G := (1/|G|) sum_{g in G} <phi(g) v | phi(g) w>. Prove that (a) <.|.>_G is again an inner product on V; (b) every phi(g) is unitary with respect to <.|.>_G, i.e. <phi(g) v | phi(g) w>_G = <v|w>_G; and (c) consequently, for any G-invariant subspace W, its orthogonal complement W^perp taken with respect to <.|.>_G is also G-invariant, so that V = W (+) W^perp as representations. Explain exactly where the ability to average over G is used.
reference_answer: (a) Each summand <phi(g)v | phi(g)w> is sesquilinear in (v,w) because phi(g) is linear and <.|.> is sesquilinear, and a finite average of sesquilinear forms is sesquilinear; Hermitian symmetry is inherited termwise. For positivity, <v|v>_G = (1/|G|) sum_g <phi(g)v | phi(g)v> >= 0 as an average of nonnegative terms, and it vanishes only if every term is 0; the g = e term gives <v|v> = 0, hence v = 0 since <.|.> is definite. So <.|.>_G is a genuine inner product. (b) Fix h in G. Then <phi(h)v | phi(h)w>_G = (1/|G|) sum_g <phi(g)phi(h)v | phi(g)phi(h)w> = (1/|G|) sum_g <phi(gh)v | phi(gh)w> by the homomorphism property. As g ranges over G so does g' = gh (left translation is a bijection of G), so the sum equals <v|w>_G. Thus phi(h) preserves <.|.>_G and is unitary for it. (c) Let W be G-invariant and u in W^perp. For any g and w in W, <phi(g)u | w>_G = <u | phi(g)^* w>_G = <u | phi(g^{-1}) w>_G, using that the adjoint of the <.|.>_G-unitary phi(g) is phi(g)^{-1} = phi(g^{-1}). Invariance gives phi(g^{-1}) w in W, so the pairing is 0; hence phi(g)u in W^perp and W^perp is invariant. Then V = W (+) W^perp (nondegeneracy) with both summands invariant, a decomposition of representations. The averaging over G is used exactly twice: forming the normalized sum (1/|G|) sum_g requires it to be finite (compact groups replace it by Haar integration), and the reindexing g -> gh being a bijection is what makes the form G-invariant.

question: Let (phi, V) be a representation of a finite group G over a field whose characteristic does not divide |G|, and let W be a G-invariant subspace with some (not necessarily invariant) projection P_W onto W (P_W^2 = P_W, im P_W = W). Define Q_W := (1/|G|) sum_{g in G} phi(g) P_W phi(g)^{-1}. Prove that Q_W commutes with every phi(g), that im Q_W = W and Q_W is a projection, and conclude that ker Q_W is a G-invariant complement, so V = W (+) ker Q_W as representations. Indicate where the hypothesis on the characteristic is used.
reference_answer: Equivariance: for h in G, phi(h) Q_W phi(h)^{-1} = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(h)phi(g) P_W phi(g)^{-1} phi(h)^{-1} = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(hg) P_W phi(hg)^{-1}. Reindexing g' = hg (a bijection of G) shows this equals Q_W, so phi(h) Q_W = Q_W phi(h) for all h. Image in W: invariance means phi(g)^{-1} maps V into V, P_W maps into W, and phi(g) maps W into W, so each term phi(g) P_W phi(g)^{-1} has image in W; the average does too, giving im Q_W subset W. Q_W fixes W pointwise: for w in W, phi(g)^{-1} w in W, P_W fixes it, and phi(g) phi(g)^{-1} w = w, so each term returns w; the normalized average (1/|G|) sum_g w = w. This normalization is exactly where the characteristic hypothesis enters: 1/|G| must exist in the field, i.e. |G| must be invertible, which holds iff the characteristic does not divide |G|. Hence Q_W|_W = id_W, so Q_W maps everything into W and acts as the identity there, giving Q_W^2 = Q_W: a projection onto W. Finally, since Q_W commutes with all phi(g), both im Q_W = W and ker Q_W are G-invariant, and V = im Q_W (+) ker Q_W = W (+) ker Q_W. Thus W has a G-invariant complement and the decomposition is of representations.

question: Let (phi_1, V_1) and (phi_2, V_2) be irreducible representations of a group G and let f: V_1 -> V_2 be G-equivariant, meaning f . phi_1(g) = phi_2(g) . f for all g in G. Prove that either f = 0 or f is an isomorphism (so V_1 ~ V_2). Your proof must show that ker f is a G-invariant subspace of V_1 and that im f is a G-invariant subspace of V_2, and then use irreducibility to force the conclusion.
reference_answer: ker f is G-invariant: take v in ker f and g in G. Then f(phi_1(g) v) = phi_2(g)(f(v)) = phi_2(g)(0) = 0, using equivariance and f(v) = 0; so phi_1(g) v in ker f. Since V_1 is irreducible, its only invariant subspaces are {0} and V_1, so either ker f = V_1 (f = 0) or ker f = {0} (f injective). im f is G-invariant: any element of im f is f(v), and phi_2(g)(f(v)) = f(phi_1(g) v) in im f by equivariance, so phi_2(g) maps im f into im f. Irreducibility of V_2 forces im f = {0} or im f = V_2. If f is not the zero map, then ker f = {0} (injective) and im f is not {0}, hence im f = V_2 (surjective). An injective and surjective linear map is a bijection, i.e. a vector-space isomorphism; it intertwines phi_1 and phi_2, so it is an isomorphism of representations and V_1 ~ V_2. Therefore f = 0 or f is an isomorphism, with no middle case. The only properties used are equivariance (invariance of kernel and image) and irreducibility (no nontrivial invariant subspaces); no field assumption is needed for this part.

question: Let (phi, V) be an irreducible representation of a group G on a finite-dimensional vector space V over an algebraically closed field F (for example F = C), and let f: V -> V be G-equivariant, i.e. f . phi(g) = phi(g) . f for all g. Prove that f = lambda . 1_V for some scalar lambda in F. Make explicit where algebraic closure and finite dimension are used, and derive as a corollary that any operator X commuting with an irreducible representation is a scalar multiple of the identity.
reference_answer: Because F is algebraically closed and V is finite-dimensional, the characteristic polynomial of f has a root in F, so f has an eigenvalue lambda in F; this is exactly where both hypotheses are needed (over R or in infinite dimension an operator may have no eigenvalue). Set f' := f - lambda . 1_V. Since 1_V commutes with every phi(g) and f is equivariant, f' phi(g) = f phi(g) - lambda phi(g) = phi(g) f - lambda phi(g) = phi(g) f', so f' is G-equivariant. Moreover f' is not invertible: lambda is an eigenvalue, so some nonzero v has (f - lambda)v = 0, giving ker f' != {0}. By part (i) of Schur's Lemma applied to the equivariant endomorphism f' on the irreducible V, f' is either zero or an isomorphism; being non-invertible, it must be zero. Hence f = lambda . 1_V. Corollary: if X satisfies phi(g) X = X phi(g) for all g, then X is a G-equivariant endomorphism of the irreducible V, so X = lambda . 1_V for some lambda; i.e. the commutant of an irreducible representation consists only of scalar multiples of the identity.

question: Let G be an abelian group. Prove that every complex irreducible representation (phi, V) of G is one-dimensional. You may use Schur's Lemma. Make clear exactly where commutativity of G and where the complex (algebraically closed) field are used, and explain why the statement can fail if the field is not algebraically closed.
reference_answer: Fix h in G. Because G is abelian, for every g in G, phi(g) phi(h) = phi(gh) = phi(hg) = phi(h) phi(g); thus the single operator phi(h) commutes with every phi(g), so phi(h) is a G-equivariant endomorphism of V. Since V is irreducible and the field is C (algebraically closed), Schur (ii) gives phi(h) = lambda_h . 1_V for some lambda_h in C. This holds for every h in G, so every representation operator is a scalar multiple of the identity. Hence for any nonzero v in V and any h, phi(h) v = lambda_h v lies in span(v), so span(v) is a G-invariant subspace. By irreducibility the only nonzero invariant subspace is V, so V = span(v) is one-dimensional. Commutativity is used to make each phi(h) commute with all phi(g) (so Schur applies to phi(h) itself); algebraic closure is used in Schur (ii) to turn phi(h) into a genuine scalar. Over a non-algebraically-closed field the conclusion fails: a generic rotation representation of a cyclic group on R^2 is irreducible over R (a non-trivial rotation has no real eigenvector, hence no proper real invariant subspace) yet is two-dimensional, precisely because the rotation operator is not a real scalar.

question: Let rho be any single-qubit density matrix (a 2x2 positive semidefinite operator with trace 1). Using the fact that the Pauli operators {1, X, Y, Z} generate an irreducible representation of the single-qubit Pauli group acting on C^2, prove that (1/4)(rho + X rho X + Y rho Y + Z rho Z) = (1/2) 1. Base your argument on Schur's Lemma / the commutant-is-scalars corollary and on the trace, not on a brute-force coordinate computation.
reference_answer: Write T(rho) := (1/4)(rho + X rho X + Y rho Y + Z rho Z); each P in {1,X,Y,Z} is Hermitian and unitary, so P rho P^dagger = P rho P. Claim: T(rho) commutes with the Pauli representation. It suffices to check commutation with each generator Q in {X,Y,Z}. Conjugating, Q T(rho) Q = (1/4) sum_P (QP) rho (QP), and as P ranges over {1,X,Y,Z} the products QP range over {1,X,Y,Z} up to overall phases (Pauli-group multiplication permutes the four classes). Since P rho P^dagger is insensitive to a global phase on P (phases cancel between P and P^dagger), the multiset {QP rho (QP)^dagger} equals {P rho P}, so Q T(rho) Q = T(rho), i.e. Q T(rho) = T(rho) Q. Thus T(rho) commutes with the generators, hence with the whole irreducible Pauli representation on C^2. By the Schur commutant corollary (commutant of an irrep = scalars), T(rho) = lambda . 1. Fix lambda by the trace: tr T(rho) = (1/4)(tr rho + tr(X rho X) + tr(Y rho Y) + tr(Z rho Z)) = (1/4)(1+1+1+1) = 1, using cyclicity and P^2 = 1 so tr(P rho P) = tr(rho) = 1. Also tr(lambda 1) = 2 lambda, so 2 lambda = 1, lambda = 1/2. Therefore T(rho) = (1/2) 1, the maximally mixed state. The argument used only irreducibility (via Schur) and trace normalization, not the entries of rho - which is the content of the symmetrization principle.

question: Let (phi, V) be a finite-dimensional representation of a group G and define its character by chi(g) := tr(phi(g)). Prove that (a) chi is a class function, i.e. chi(h g h^{-1}) = chi(g) for all g, h in G, and (b) chi(e) = dim V. State precisely which properties of the trace and which property of phi you use, and explain why being a class function means chi is really a function on conjugacy classes.
reference_answer: (a) Fix g, h in G. Using multiplicativity of phi, phi(h g h^{-1}) = phi(h) phi(g) phi(h^{-1}) = phi(h) phi(g) phi(h)^{-1}, the last equality from phi(h^{-1}) = phi(h)^{-1} (valid for any representation). Apply the trace: chi(h g h^{-1}) = tr(phi(h) phi(g) phi(h)^{-1}). By cyclicity of the trace, tr(A B A^{-1}) = tr(A^{-1} A B) = tr(B) with A = phi(h), B = phi(g), so this equals tr(phi(g)) = chi(g). Hence chi is constant on each conjugacy class {h g h^{-1} : h in G}, i.e. a class function; equivalently chi descends to a well-defined function on the set of conjugacy classes of G. The trace properties used are linearity (to define tr) and cyclicity tr(AB) = tr(BA); the property of phi used is multiplicativity phi(xy) = phi(x)phi(y) together with phi(h^{-1}) = phi(h)^{-1}. (b) Since phi(e) = 1_V (a representation sends the identity to the identity operator), chi(e) = tr(1_V) = dim V, as the trace of the identity on an n-dimensional space is n. So the character at the identity recovers the degree of the representation.

question: Let G be a finite group and let the characters of its pairwise inequivalent complex irreducible representations W_1, ..., W_k be chi_1, ..., chi_k, orthonormal for the inner product (x, y) = (1/|G|) sum_{g} conj(x(g)) y(g); so (chi_i, chi_j) = delta_{ij}. Let (phi, V) be an arbitrary finite-dimensional complex representation with isotypical decomposition V ~ (+)_i W_i^{(+) n_i} (n_i the multiplicity of W_i). Prove that n_i = (chi_i, chi_V), where chi_V is the character of V. Then prove the two consequences: V is irreducible iff (chi_V, chi_V) = 1, and two representations are isomorphic iff they have equal characters.
reference_answer: By additivity of the character under direct sums (chi_{A (+) B} = chi_A + chi_B, which follows from tr being additive on block-diagonal operators), the isotypical decomposition V ~ (+)_j W_j^{(+) n_j} gives chi_V = sum_j n_j chi_j. Taking the inner product with chi_i and using bilinearity (conjugate-linearity in the first slot but the n_j are real nonnegative integers) together with orthonormality, (chi_i, chi_V) = (chi_i, sum_j n_j chi_j) = sum_j n_j (chi_i, chi_j) = sum_j n_j delta_{ij} = n_i. This proves the multiplicity formula. Consequence 1: compute (chi_V, chi_V) = (sum_i n_i chi_i, sum_j n_j chi_j) = sum_{i,j} n_i n_j delta_{ij} = sum_i n_i^2. Since the n_i are nonnegative integers, sum_i n_i^2 = 1 holds iff exactly one n_i equals 1 and all others are 0, i.e. iff V is (isomorphic to) a single irreducible W_i; thus V is irreducible iff (chi_V, chi_V) = 1. Consequence 2: if V ~ V' then they have the same character (characters are isomorphism invariants, since conjugate representation matrices have equal trace). Conversely, the multiplicities n_i = (chi_i, chi_V) are determined entirely by chi_V; so if chi_V = chi_{V'} then n_i(V) = n_i(V') for all i, meaning V and V' have the same isotypical decomposition and hence V ~ V'. Therefore two representations are isomorphic iff their characters coincide.

question: Let (phi, V) be a finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group G, and let ( phi_U, U) be a complex irreducible representation of G. Recall that Hom_G(U, V) is the space of intertwiners f: U -> V, i.e. linear maps satisfying f . phi_U(g) = phi(g) . f for all g, and that Hom_G is additive in each argument: Hom_G(X, Y (+) Z) ~ Hom_G(X, Y) (+) Hom_G(X, Z). Prove that dim Hom_G(U, V) equals the multiplicity k of U in the isotypical decomposition of V. You should use Schur's Lemma to evaluate Hom_G(U, U) and Hom_G(U, F) where F collects the irreducible summands of V inequivalent to U.
reference_answer: Decompose V ~ V_U (+) F, where V_U ~ U^{(+)k} is the isotypical component of U (U appearing with multiplicity k) and F is the direct sum of all irreducible summands of V inequivalent to U. By additivity of Hom_G in the second argument, Hom_G(U, V) ~ Hom_G(U, U^{(+)k}) (+) Hom_G(U, F) ~ ((+)_{i=1}^{k} Hom_G(U, U)) (+) Hom_G(U, F). Now evaluate the pieces with Schur's Lemma. First, Hom_G(U, U) is the space of G-equivariant endomorphisms of the irreducible U over C; by Schur (ii) every such endomorphism is a scalar multiple of 1_U, so Hom_G(U, U) = C . 1_U has dimension 1. Second, for any irreducible summand W of F, W is inequivalent to U, so by Schur (i) any equivariant map U -> W is either zero or an isomorphism; an isomorphism would make U ~ W, contradicting inequivalence, so the only equivariant map is 0. Hence Hom_G(U, W) = 0 for each such W, and by additivity Hom_G(U, F) = 0. Combining, dim Hom_G(U, V) = sum_{i=1}^{k} dim Hom_G(U, U) + dim Hom_G(U, F) = k . 1 + 0 = k. Therefore the dimension of the intertwiner space Hom_G(U, V) equals the multiplicity of U in V, which realizes the multiplicity space of U as the space of intertwiners from U into V.

question: Let (phi, V) be a finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group G, and for X in L(V) define the symmetrized operator Xbar := (1/|G|) sum_{g in G} phi(g) X phi(g)^{-1}. (a) Prove that Xbar is G-invariant, i.e. phi(h) Xbar = Xbar phi(h) for all h in G. (b) Using Schur's Lemma, prove that if V = W_1 (+) W_2 is a multiplicity-free decomposition into two inequivalent irreducibles, then in a basis adapted to W_1, W_2 the operator Xbar is block diagonal with each diagonal block a scalar multiple of the identity, and the off-diagonal blocks vanish. Explain which part of Schur kills the off-diagonal blocks and which part scalarizes the diagonal blocks.
reference_answer: (a) For h in G, phi(h) Xbar phi(h)^{-1} = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(h)phi(g) X phi(g)^{-1}phi(h)^{-1} = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(hg) X phi(hg)^{-1}. Reindexing g' = hg (a bijection of G) leaves the average unchanged, so phi(h) Xbar phi(h)^{-1} = Xbar, i.e. phi(h) Xbar = Xbar phi(h). Thus Xbar commutes with the whole representation; it is G-equivariant. (b) Write Xbar in block form with respect to V = W_1 (+) W_2: Xbar = [[A_{11}, A_{12}], [A_{21}, A_{22}]], where A_{ij}: W_j -> W_i. Equivariance phi(h) Xbar = Xbar phi(h) restricted to blocks says A_{ij} phi_j(h) = phi_i(h) A_{ij} for all h, i.e. each A_{ij} is an intertwiner from the irreducible W_j to the irreducible W_i. For the off-diagonal blocks i != j: W_1 and W_2 are inequivalent irreducibles, so by Schur part (i) any intertwiner between them is zero; hence A_{12} = 0 and A_{21} = 0. For the diagonal blocks i = j: A_{ii} is an equivariant endomorphism of the irreducible W_i over C, so by Schur part (ii) A_{ii} = lambda_i . 1_{W_i} for some scalar lambda_i. Therefore Xbar = lambda_1 1_{W_1} (+) lambda_2 1_{W_2}, block diagonal with scalar blocks. Part (i) of Schur kills the off-diagonal blocks (maps between inequivalent irreps), and part (ii) scalarizes the diagonal blocks (equivariant endomorphisms of an irrep). This is exactly the small multiplicity-free instance of the general symmetrization result; with multiplicities the diagonal blocks would instead be 1_{W_k} tensored with an arbitrary operator on the multiplicity space.

question: Let (phi, V) be a representation of a group G and consider the tensor-square representation on V (x) V with the swap operator F defined by F(|x> (x) |y>) = |y> (x) |x>, extended linearly. (a) Prove F^2 = 1 and that F commutes with phi(g) (x) phi(g) for all g. (b) Define Pi_sym := (1/2)(1 + F) and Pi_asym := (1/2)(1 - F). Prove that Pi_sym and Pi_asym are orthogonal projections with Pi_sym + Pi_asym = 1 and Pi_sym Pi_asym = 0, that their images are exactly the +1 and -1 eigenspaces of F, and that both images are G-invariant subspaces, giving V (x) V = Sym^2(V) (+) Lambda^2(V) as representations.
reference_answer: (a) On product vectors F(F(|x> (x) |y>)) = F(|y> (x) |x>) = |x> (x) |y>, so F^2 = 1 on a spanning set, hence everywhere by linearity; in particular F is an involution, so its only possible eigenvalues are +1 and -1. For commutation, (phi(g) (x) phi(g)) F (|x> (x) |y>) = (phi(g) (x) phi(g))(|y> (x) |x>) = phi(g)|y> (x) phi(g)|x> = F(phi(g)|x> (x) phi(g)|y>) = F (phi(g) (x) phi(g)) (|x> (x) |y>), and by linearity F commutes with phi(g) (x) phi(g) for all g. (b) Compute Pi_sym^2 = (1/4)(1 + F)^2 = (1/4)(1 + 2F + F^2) = (1/4)(2 + 2F) = (1/2)(1 + F) = Pi_sym, so Pi_sym is idempotent; similarly Pi_asym^2 = (1/4)(1 - 2F + F^2) = Pi_asym. Both are Hermitian since F is Hermitian (F = F^dagger because F is a real symmetric permutation / an involution that is also unitary, hence self-adjoint), so they are orthogonal projections. Pi_sym + Pi_asym = (1/2)(1 + F) + (1/2)(1 - F) = 1 and Pi_sym Pi_asym = (1/4)(1 + F)(1 - F) = (1/4)(1 - F^2) = (1/4)(1 - 1) = 0. Because Pi_sym Pi_asym = 0 and they sum to 1, their images are complementary. The image of Pi_sym is {|z> : F|z> = |z>} (the +1 eigenspace): if F|z> = |z> then Pi_sym|z> = |z>, and conversely any |z> in the image satisfies F|z> = F Pi_sym |z> = (1/2)(F + F^2)|z> = (1/2)(F + 1)|z> = Pi_sym|z> = |z>; likewise im Pi_asym is the -1 eigenspace. Finally, since F commutes with phi(g) (x) phi(g), so do Pi_sym and Pi_asym (they are polynomials in F), hence their images are G-invariant subspaces. question: Let (phi, V) be a finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group G. For the trivial representation, define P := (1/|G|) sum_{g in G} phi(g). Prove that (a) P is idempotent (P^2 = P), (b) im P = V^G := {|v> : phi(g)|v> = |v> for all g}, and (c) P commutes with every phi(h). Then explain, by taking the trace, why tr P equals the multiplicity of the trivial representation in V (the number of independent G-invariant vectors), connecting to the general character-projection formula P_W = (dim W / |G|) sum_g conj(chi_W(g)) phi(g).
reference_answer: (a) and (c) together: for any h in G, phi(h) P = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(h)phi(g) = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(hg) = (1/|G|) sum_{g'} phi(g') = P, reindexing g' = hg (a bijection of G); likewise P phi(h) = P by reindexing on the right. So phi(h) P = P = P phi(h) for all h, which gives both that P commutes with every phi(h) and that P is left/right absorbing for the group action. Idempotency follows: P^2 = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(g) P = (1/|G|) sum_g P = P, using phi(g) P = P from the previous line. (b) If |v> in im P, write |v> = P|w>; then phi(h)|v> = phi(h) P|w> = P|w> = |v> for all h, so |v> in V^G, giving im P subset V^G. Conversely if |v> in V^G then phi(g)|v> = |v> for all g, so P|v> = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(g)|v> = (1/|G|) sum_g |v> = |v>, hence |v> in im P; thus V^G subset im P. Therefore im P = V^G. (b continued, trace) Since P is idempotent and (being an average of the unitaries phi(g) in a suitable invariant inner product) an orthogonal projection, its trace equals the dimension of its image: tr P = dim im P = dim V^G, which is precisely the number of independent G-invariant vectors, i.e. the multiplicity of the trivial representation in V. This is the chi_W = chi_triv = 1 case of the general formula P_W = (dim W/|G|) sum_g conj(chi_W(g)) phi(g): the trivial representation has dimension 1 and character identically 1, so P_triv = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(g) = P, and its trace recovers the multiplicity, consistent with the character inner-product formula for multiplicities.

question: A student claims: for any representation (phi, V) of a finite group G and any X in L(V), the symmetrized operator Xbar = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(g) X phi(g)^{-1} is always block diagonal with respect to the isotypical decomposition AND each diagonal block is a scalar multiple of the identity. Decide whether the second half of this claim is true in general. Give an explicit counterexample using the action of S_2 = {e, (12)} on (C^2)^{(x)2} by permuting the two tensor factors (so phi((12)) = F, the swap), and explain precisely what feature of the decomposition makes the diagonal block fail to be scalar.
reference_answer: The block-diagonal part of the claim is correct, but the assertion that every diagonal block is a scalar multiple of the identity is FALSE in general; it holds only when each isotypical component is a single copy of an irrep (multiplicity one). Counterexample: let S_2 act on (C^2)^{(x)2} by phi(e) = 1 and phi((12)) = F (swap). The isotypical decomposition is (C^2)^{(x)2} = Vtriv (+) Vsgn, where Vtriv is the 3-dimensional +1 eigenspace of F (symmetric subspace, spanned by |00>, |11>, (|01>+|10>)/sqrt 2) carrying three copies of the trivial irrep, and Vsgn is the 1-dimensional -1 eigenspace (spanned by (|01>-|10>)/sqrt 2) carrying the sign irrep. Now take X = |00><11| (a rank-one operator). Symmetrizing: Xbar = (1/2)(X + F X F^{-1}) = (1/2)(|00><11| + F|00><11|F) = (1/2)(|00><11| + |00><11|) = |00><11|, because F|00> = |00> and F|11> = |11> (both symmetric), so F X F = X. The operator Xbar = |00><11| maps entirely within the symmetric (trivial-isotypical) subspace Vtriv, so it is block diagonal (its Vsgn block and the off-diagonal blocks are zero, consistent with Schur part (i)). However, restricted to the 3-dimensional Vtriv it is the rank-one operator |00><11|, which is NOT a scalar multiple of the 3x3 identity (it is not even diagonal in the symmetric basis and has rank 1, trace 0). The reason the diagonal block is not scalar is multiplicity: Vtriv contains the trivial irrep three times, so Hom_G(triv, Vtriv) is 3-dimensional and the symmetrized operator restricted to Vtriv is of the form 1_{W_triv} (x) X_triv with X_triv an arbitrary 3x3 operator on the multiplicity space C^3 - only this multiplicity-space factor is scalar when the multiplicity is 1. Hence Schur's Lemma forces scalar diagonal blocks only in the multiplicity-free case; with multiplicity greater than 1 the diagonal block is merely of the form (identity on the irrep) (x) (arbitrary operator on the multiplicity space).

question: A student asserts: the tensor product of two irreducible representations of a group G is again irreducible. Show this is false by a counterexample. Specifically, take any representation (phi, V) of G with dim V >= 2 (you may take V irreducible) and consider the tensor-square representation on V (x) V. Exhibit a proper nonzero G-invariant subspace of V (x) V, and compute the dimensions to show V (x) V cannot be irreducible when dim V >= 2.
reference_answer: The claim is false. Let (phi, V) be any representation with d := dim V >= 2 (e.g. an irreducible one such as the standard representation of S_3 of dimension 2). Consider the tensor-square representation (phi (x) phi) on V (x) V, which has dimension d^2 >= 4. The swap operator F on V (x) V, defined by F(|x> (x) |y>) = |y> (x) |x>, commutes with phi(g) (x) phi(g) for all g (shown by swapping tensor factors), and F^2 = 1. Hence the +1 eigenspace Sym^2(V) and the -1 eigenspace Lambda^2(V) of F are both G-invariant subspaces of V (x) V, and V (x) V = Sym^2(V) (+) Lambda^2(V) as representations. Their dimensions are dim Sym^2(V) = d(d+1)/2 and dim Lambda^2(V) = d(d-1)/2 (standard counts of symmetric and antisymmetric index pairs). For d >= 2 both of these are strictly positive: dim Lambda^2(V) = d(d-1)/2 >= 1 and dim Sym^2(V) = d(d+1)/2 >= 3, and both are strictly less than d^2 (since each is a proper summand of a direct sum of two nonzero spaces). Thus Lambda^2(V) is a proper nonzero G-invariant subspace of V (x) V (and so is Sym^2(V)); the existence of such a subspace means V (x) V is reducible. Therefore even when V is irreducible, V (x) V fails to be irreducible as soon as dim V >= 2, refuting the claim. (For the degenerate case d = 1, Lambda^2(V) = 0 and V (x) V ~ V is one-dimensional hence irreducible, which is exactly why the hypothesis dim V >= 2 is needed.)

question: Proposition 3.22 says the decomposition of a representation into isotypical components is unique. A student over-reads this as: 'the decomposition of a representation into irreducible subrepresentations is unique.' Show by counterexample that the finer decomposition into individual irreducible subspaces is NOT unique, even though the isotypical components are. Use the trivial-isotypical component of the S_2 action on (C^2)^{(x)2} (equivalently, any space carrying the trivial representation with multiplicity >= 2) and exhibit two genuinely different splittings into irreducible lines.
reference_answer: The student's reading is wrong: it is the isotypical components that are unique, not the splitting of a multiplicity-greater-than-one component into individual irreducible subspaces. Take the S_2 action on (C^2)^{(x)2} with phi((12)) = F. The symmetric subspace Vtriv = Sym^2(C^2) is the +1 eigenspace of F, a 3-dimensional space on which S_2 acts trivially; it is the trivial-isotypical component and is uniquely determined (it equals the +1 eigenspace of F, basis-independent). But because S_2 acts as the identity on all of Vtriv, EVERY one-dimensional subspace of Vtriv is an irreducible (trivial) subrepresentation, and Vtriv can be written as a direct sum of three trivial lines in infinitely many ways. Concretely, one splitting is Vtriv = span(|00>) (+) span(|11>) (+) span((|01>+|10>)/sqrt 2); a genuinely different splitting is Vtriv = span((|00>+|11>)/sqrt 2) (+) span((|00>-|11>)/sqrt 2) (+) span((|01>+|10>)/sqrt 2). Both are decompositions of Vtriv into three irreducible (trivial) subrepresentations, but the first line span(|00>) of the first splitting is not among the lines of the second splitting, so the two decompositions into irreducibles are different. This does not contradict Proposition 3.22: the isotypical component Vtriv itself is identical in both (it is the full +1 eigenspace of F), and only its internal basis / line-by-line splitting changed. The source of the non-uniqueness is multiplicity: when an irrep occurs with multiplicity n >= 2, the choice of the n individual copies corresponds to a choice of basis of the n-dimensional multiplicity space, and any invertible change of that basis gives an equally valid finer decomposition. Uniqueness is recovered precisely in the multiplicity-free case.

question: A student claims: 'every finite-dimensional representation of every group can be made unitary by averaging an inner product over the group, so every invariant subspace has an invariant complement.' Explain why the averaging argument requires the group to be finite (or compact, with Haar measure), and give a counterexample: a finite-dimensional representation of an infinite group that has an invariant subspace with NO invariant complement (hence is not unitarizable and not completely reducible).
reference_answer: The averaging argument defines <v|w>_G = (1/|G|) sum_{g in G} <phi(g)v | phi(g)w> (finite groups) or integrates against the Haar probability measure (compact groups). It needs the normalized average/integral to exist and to be invariant under the reindexing g -> gh; for a general infinite non-compact group there is no finite normalization and no invariant probability measure, so the construction breaks down. Counterexample: let G = (R, +), an infinite non-compact group, and define phi: R -> GL(2, C) by phi(t) = [[1, t], [0, 1]]. This is a representation since phi(s) phi(t) = [[1, s+t],[0,1]] = phi(s+t). Consider W = span(e_1), the first coordinate line. W is G-invariant: phi(t) e_1 = e_1 for all t, so W is a (trivial) subrepresentation. Suppose for contradiction there were a G-invariant complement W' with C^2 = W (+) W', dim W' = 1, say W' = span(v) with v = (a, b), b != 0 (if b = 0 then v in W, impossible). Invariance of W' requires phi(t) v in W' = span(v) for all t, i.e. phi(t) v = lambda(t) v. But phi(t)(a, b) = (a + t b, b), and for this to be a scalar multiple of (a, b) we need (a + t b, b) = lambda(t)(a, b); the second coordinate forces lambda(t) = 1, and then the first forces a + t b = a, i.e. t b = 0 for all t, impossible since b != 0 and t ranges over all reals. Hence no one-dimensional invariant complement exists, so W has no invariant complement and phi is not completely reducible; equivalently phi is not unitarizable (a unitary representation would decompose W^perp as an invariant complement). This shows the finite/compact hypothesis is essential: the only G-invariant subspaces of this phi are {0}, W, and C^2, and W cannot be split off invariantly. For finite or compact groups the averaging restores complete reducibility, which is exactly why those hypotheses appear in Maschke's theorem and its compact-group analogue.

question: Part (ii) of Schur's Lemma concludes that a G-equivariant endomorphism of an irreducible representation is a scalar multiple of the identity, under the hypothesis that the field is algebraically closed. Delineate the boundary of this result: show precisely why algebraic closure is needed by exhibiting an irreducible real representation whose equivariant endomorphism algebra (commutant) is strictly larger than the real scalars, and state what part (i) still guarantees without algebraic closure.
reference_answer: Part (i) of Schur (a nonzero equivariant map between irreps is an isomorphism; an equivariant endomorphism of an irrep is 0 or invertible) holds over ANY field, because it uses only invariance of kernel and image. Part (ii) additionally needs an eigenvalue in the field, which is where algebraic closure is essential: without it an equivariant endomorphism may be invertible yet not scalar. Boundary example: let G = Z/4 = <g> act on V = R^2 by phi(g) = R, the 90-degree rotation [[0, -1], [1, 0]]. This representation is irreducible over R: R has no real eigenvector (its eigenvalues are +-i, not real), so there is no proper nonzero real invariant subspace. Now consider the commutant, the real-linear maps A with A R = R A. The rotation R itself satisfies R R = R R trivially, and R is NOT a real scalar multiple of the identity (a real scalar times the identity is diagonal, but R has zero diagonal and nonzero off-diagonal). More fully, the commutant of R over R is {a I + b R : a, b in R}, which is a 2-dimensional real algebra isomorphic to the complex numbers C (with R playing the role of i), strictly larger than the real scalars R I. Thus over R an equivariant endomorphism of this irreducible representation need not be scalar, so Schur (ii) genuinely fails without algebraic closure. What survives from part (i): every nonzero element of this commutant is invertible (indeed a I + b R has determinant a^2 + b^2 > 0 unless a = b = 0), so the commutant is a division algebra - consistent with the general fact (Schur part (i)) that the endomorphism algebra of an irreducible representation is a division ring. Over an algebraically closed field this division ring collapses to the field itself (scalars), recovering part (ii); over R it can be R, C, or the quaternions H (the real/complex/quaternionic types), and this example realizes the complex type.

question: Many representation-theoretic results for finite groups (invariant complements, complete reducibility, character orthogonality) are proved using the averaging (1/|G|) sum_{g in G}. For compact groups this is replaced by integration against the Haar probability measure. Delineate carefully which statements carry over verbatim to infinite compact groups and which must be modified or fail. In particular address: (a) existence of invariant complements and complete reducibility; (b) finite-dimensionality of irreducible representations; (c) the identity sum_i (dim W_i)^2 = |G| and formulas explicitly involving |G|.
reference_answer: The key replacement is: the normalized finite average (1/|G|) sum_g, which is an invariant probability measure on a finite group, becomes the Haar integral integral_G . dg against the unique invariant probability measure dg guaranteed for any compact group (invariant under left and right translation, normalized so integral_G 1 dg = 1). Wherever a proof used only the invariance and normalization of the average, it carries over verbatim with sum replaced by integral. (a) Invariant complements and complete reducibility DO carry over: the Weyl unitarity trick defines <v|w>_G = integral_G <phi(g)v | phi(g)w> dg, which is still a well-defined G-invariant inner product (the integrand is continuous and the measure finite), making phi unitary and giving every invariant subspace an invariant complement; thus every finite-dimensional representation over C of a compact group is completely reducible - verbatim analogue of Maschke. (b) Finite-dimensionality of irreducibles: for FINITE groups every irrep is automatically finite-dimensional (it is a subrepresentation of the finite-dimensional regular representation). For infinite compact groups one must RESTRICT attention or prove a theorem: it is a nontrivial theorem (Peter-Weyl) that every irreducible UNITARY representation of a compact group is finite-dimensional; this does not come for free from averaging and is a genuine modification of the finite-group situation (where it was trivial). (c) Formulas with |G| must be modified or fail: the identity sum_i (dim W_i)^2 = |G| and 'multiplicity of W_i in the regular representation equals dim W_i summing to |G|' involve the finite cardinality |G|, which is infinite for an infinite compact group. The regular representation becomes L^2(G), which is infinite-dimensional when G is infinite; the correct compact-group statement is that L^2(G) decomposes as a Hilbert-space direct sum of all irreducible unitary representations, each with multiplicity equal to its dimension (Peter-Weyl), and the matrix coefficients form an orthonormal basis - but any expression literally equal to |G| is no longer valid. Character orthogonality (chi_i, chi_j) = delta_{ij} survives with the inner product (x,y) = integral_G conj(x(g)) y(g) dg, since it too used only invariance/normalization; however the counting statement 'number of irreps = number of conjugacy classes' and sums over the finite group do not transfer. Summary: averaging-based existence results (invariant complements, complete reducibility, character orthonormality) carry over by replacing sum with the Haar integral; statements relying on the finiteness of |G| (the dimension-squared sum, finite-dimensional regular representation) fail and are replaced by Peter-Weyl, and finite-dimensionality of irreducibles becomes a theorem rather than an automatic fact.

question: For a finite-dimensional representation (phi, V) of a group G, the dual representation (phi^*, V^*) is defined by phi^*(g)(L) = L . phi(g)^{-1}. (a) Prove that in a basis phi^*(g) = phi(g^{-1})^T, and that if (phi, V) is unitary then phi^*(g) = conj(phi(g)) (the entrywise complex conjugate). (b) Delineate the boundary between a representation and its dual: give the character relation chi_{V^*}(g) = conj(chi_V(g)) for unitary representations, and explain precisely when V is isomorphic to its dual (self-dual) versus not, giving an explicit example of a NON-self-dual irreducible representation. (c) State what remains true regardless: (phi^*, V^*) is irreducible iff (phi, V) is.
reference_answer: (a) By definition phi^*(g)(L) = L . phi(g)^{-1} for L in V^*. Fixing dual bases, the matrix of the map L -> L . phi(g)^{-1} acting on row vectors is right multiplication by phi(g)^{-1}, which on column-vector (coordinate) representation of V^* is the transpose: phi^*(g) = (phi(g)^{-1})^T = phi(g^{-1})^T, using phi(g)^{-1} = phi(g^{-1}). If (phi, V) is unitary, then phi(g)^{-1} = phi(g)^dagger = conj(phi(g))^T, so phi(g^{-1})^T = (phi(g)^dagger)^T = (conj(phi(g))^T)^T = conj(phi(g)); hence phi^*(g) = conj(phi(g)), the entrywise complex conjugate. (b) Taking traces of the character: chi_{V^*}(g) = tr(phi^*(g)) = tr(phi(g^{-1})^T) = tr(phi(g^{-1})) = chi_V(g^{-1}); for unitary phi this equals conj(chi_V(g)) because chi_V(g^{-1}) = conj(chi_V(g)) for unitary representations (eigenvalues of phi(g) lie on the unit circle, so inverse = conjugate). Thus chi_{V^*}(g) = conj(chi_V(g)). The boundary: V is self-dual (V ~ V^*) iff chi_V = chi_{V^*}, i.e. iff chi_V(g) = conj(chi_V(g)) for all g, i.e. iff the character is real-valued. So real-character (in particular all-real-matrix, e.g. permutation) representations are self-dual, while a representation with a genuinely complex character is NOT self-dual. Explicit non-self-dual example: let G = Z/3 = <g> and let (phi, C) be the one-dimensional irrep phi(g) = omega, where omega = e^{2 pi i/3} is a primitive cube root of unity. Its character is chi(g) = omega, which is not real (omega != conj(omega) = omega^2). Its dual is phi^*(g) = conj(omega) = omega^2, the OTHER nontrivial irrep of Z/3; since omega != omega^2, phi and phi^* have different characters and are inequivalent, so this irrep is not self-dual. (c) Regardless of self-duality, (phi^*, V^*) is irreducible iff (phi, V) is: invariant subspaces of V^* correspond (via annihilators) bijectively and inclusion-reversingly to invariant subspaces of V, so V^* has only the trivial invariant subspaces iff V does. Hence duality preserves irreducibility even when it changes the isomorphism class.

question: A POVM P = {P_i : i in [2^m]} is implemented through block encodings as follows. For each outcome i we are given a unitary U_i that is a (beta, a)-block-encoding of sqrt(P_i), all sharing the SAME ancilla size a and the SAME subnormalization factor beta > 0, so that U_i |0^a> |psi> = (1/beta) |0^a> sqrt(P_i) |psi> + |perp_i>, where (<0^a| tensor I)|perp_i> = 0. Define the controlled unitary W = sum_i |i><i| tensor U_i acting on an output register in the uniform superposition |u> = (1/sqrt(2^m)) sum_i |i>, an ancilla register |0^a>, and the system register |psi>. After applying W one measures the ancilla register and postselects on the outcome 0^a. Starting from |u> |0^a> |psi>, derive in full the probability P(succ) of obtaining 0^a on the ancilla, show that it equals exactly 1/(beta^2 2^m) independent of the input state |psi>, and identify precisely where the POVM completeness relation sum_i P_i = I and the mutual orthogonality of the output-register basis states are used.
reference_answer: Apply W to the uniform-superposition input. Because W is block-diagonal in the output register, W |u> |0^a> |psi> = (1/sqrt(2^m)) sum_i |i> (U_i |0^a> |psi>) = (1/(beta sqrt(2^m))) sum_i |i> |0^a> sqrt(P_i)|psi> + |perp>, where |perp> = (1/sqrt(2^m)) sum_i |i> |perp_i> satisfies (I tensor <0^a| tensor I)|perp> = 0 because each (<0^a| tensor I)|perp_i> = 0. Postselecting the ancilla on 0^a projects out |perp> entirely, since |perp> has zero overlap with the subspace spanned by |0^a> on the ancilla. The unnormalized postselected vector is therefore (1/(beta sqrt(2^m))) sum_i |i> |0^a> sqrt(P_i)|psi>. Its squared norm is the success probability. The output-register states |i> are mutually orthonormal, so the cross terms vanish and the norm squared factorizes outcome by outcome: P(succ) = (1/(beta^2 2^m)) sum_i || sqrt(P_i)|psi> ||^2 = (1/(beta^2 2^m)) sum_i <psi| sqrt(P_i)^dagger sqrt(P_i) |psi> = (1/(beta^2 2^m)) sum_i <psi| P_i |psi>. Here we used sqrt(P_i)^dagger sqrt(P_i) = P_i because each P_i is positive semidefinite and sqrt(P_i) is its unique PSD square root. Finally, by POVM completeness sum_i P_i = I, so sum_i <psi| P_i |psi> = <psi| I |psi> = 1 for any normalized |psi>. Hence P(succ) = 1/(beta^2 2^m), which is manifestly independent of |psi>. Completeness is what collapses the state-dependent sum to the constant 1; the orthogonality of the |i> is what prevents interference between different outcomes so the sum of norms (not a norm of a sum) appears.

question: In the block-encoding implementation of a 2^m-outcome POVM via W = sum_i |i><i| tensor U_i (each U_i a (beta,a)-block-encoding of sqrt(P_i)), a single run succeeds (ancilla returns 0^a) with probability P(succ) = 1/(beta^2 2^m). Explain quantitatively why naive repetition is wasteful, and show that amplitude amplification raises the success probability to a constant while using only O(beta 2^{m/2} log(1/delta)) queries to W and W^dagger to reach failure probability at most delta. State clearly which quantity plays the role of the 'good' amplitude, why the amplification cost scales as 1/sqrt(P(succ)), and where the logarithmic factor log(1/delta) comes from.
reference_answer: Naive repetition: a single run flags success with probability p := P(succ) = 1/(beta^2 2^m), so the expected number of independent repetitions to see one success is 1/p = beta^2 2^m, which grows exponentially in m. Each repetition uses O(1) queries to W, so naive repetition costs O(beta^2 2^m) queries. Amplitude amplification: the postselected run prepares a state of the form sqrt(p) |good> + sqrt(1-p) |bad>, where |good> is the normalized component with the ancilla equal to 0^a (the 'good' amplitude is sqrt(p)). Standard amplitude amplification applies O(1/sqrt(p)) rounds, each round being one call to the preparation unitary (built from W) and its inverse (hence W^dagger), interleaved with reflections about |good> and about the initial state. After O(1/sqrt(p)) = O(beta 2^{m/2}) rounds the amplitude of |good> is rotated to Theta(1), so a single final measurement succeeds with constant probability. The quadratic speedup is exactly the replacement of 1/p (classical) by 1/sqrt(p) (quantum): amplitude amplification rotates an angle theta with sin^2(theta) = p by equal increments, and reaching angle pi/2 needs O(1/theta) = O(1/sqrt(p)) steps since theta ~ sqrt(p) for small p. The log(1/delta) factor: one amplified round still leaves a constant failure probability c < 1; to drive the total failure probability below delta one repeats the amplified procedure O(log(1/delta)) times (majority/until-success), each repetition independently failing with probability at most c, so c^{O(log(1/delta))} <= delta. Multiplying the per-amplification cost O(beta 2^{m/2}) by the O(log(1/delta)) outer repetitions gives the total query count O(beta 2^{m/2} log(1/delta)) to W and W^dagger.

question: Two normalized but possibly non-orthogonal pure states |psi> and |phi> are given with overlap c := <psi|phi>, |c| < 1, and we are promised the unknown state is one of them. Consider the three-element POVM with P_psi = (1/(1+|c|)) |phi_perp><phi_perp|, P_phi = (1/(1+|c|)) |psi_perp><psi_perp|, and P_? = I - P_psi - P_phi, where |psi_perp> := (|phi> - c|psi>)/sqrt(1-|c|^2) and |phi_perp> := (|psi> - c*|phi>)/sqrt(1-|c|^2). Demonstrate by a concrete counterexample-style argument that NO two-element POVM {E_psi, E_phi} (with only the two conclusive labels and no inconclusive outcome) can be unambiguous, i.e. cannot simultaneously satisfy <phi|E_psi|phi> = 0 and <psi|E_phi|psi> = 0 while being a valid POVM, whenever 0 < |c| < 1. Then verify that the given three-element POVM is unambiguous and explain why introducing P_? is exactly the structural escape that restores validity.
reference_answer: Unambiguity requires E_psi to never fire on phi and E_phi to never fire on psi: <phi|E_psi|phi> = 0 and <psi|E_phi|psi> = 0. Since E_psi, E_phi are PSD, <phi|E_psi|phi> = 0 forces E_psi|phi> = 0 (a PSD operator with zero expectation on a vector annihilates it), so range(E_psi) is orthogonal to |phi>; in the two-dimensional span{|psi>,|phi>} this means E_psi is supported on the one-dimensional complement of |phi>, i.e. E_psi = a |phi_perp><phi_perp| for some a >= 0. Likewise E_phi = b |psi_perp><psi_perp|, b >= 0. A two-element POVM must satisfy completeness E_psi + E_phi = I on span{|psi>,|phi>}. Take the matrix element in state |psi>: <psi|E_psi|psi> + <psi|E_phi|psi> = <psi|I|psi> = 1. But <psi|E_phi|psi> = 0 by unambiguity, so <psi|E_psi|psi> = 1. Now <psi|E_psi|psi> = a |<psi|phi_perp>|^2. Compute <psi|phi_perp> = (<psi|psi> - c<psi|phi>)/sqrt(1-|c|^2) = (1 - |c|^2)/sqrt(1-|c|^2) = sqrt(1-|c|^2). So a (1-|c|^2) = 1, giving a = 1/(1-|c|^2). By symmetry b = 1/(1-|c|^2). Then E_psi + E_phi = (1/(1-|c|^2)) (|phi_perp><phi_perp| + |psi_perp><psi_perp|). This operator does NOT equal I when c != 0: its trace is 2/(1-|c|^2) > 2 = Tr(I on the 2D space) whenever |c| > 0, so E_psi + E_phi != I. Hence no valid two-element unambiguous POVM exists for 0 < |c| < 1 -- completeness is violated because the two rank-one effects are forced to be too 'heavy'. The fix: keep P_psi, P_phi rank-one on |phi_perp>, |psi_perp> but SHRINK their weights to 1/(1+|c|) (instead of the forced 1/(1-|c|^2) = 1/((1-|c|)(1+|c|))), and absorb the deficit into P_? = I - P_psi - P_phi. One checks P_psi, P_phi >= 0 trivially, and P_? >= 0 because the weight 1/(1+|c|) is small enough (the eigenvalues of P_psi+P_phi on the 2D space are (1 +/- |c|)/(1+|c|), so its operator norm is exactly 1 and I - (P_psi+P_phi) >= 0). Unambiguity still holds: <phi|P_psi|phi> ∝ |<phi|phi_perp>|^2 = 0 and <psi|P_phi|psi> ∝ |<psi|psi_perp>|^2 = 0. Thus the inconclusive outcome P_? is not cosmetic: it is the exact slack that lets positivity and completeness coexist with unambiguity once the states overlap.

reviews.notes: Example 9.14 impossibility (counterexample). Verified numerically for c in {0.3,0.6i,0.8}: PSD zero-expectation forces E_psi=a|phi_perp><phi_perp|, E_phi=b|psi_perp><psi_perp|; <psi|phi_perp>=sqrt(1-|c|^2) gives a=b=1/(1-|c|^2); Tr(E_psi+E_phi)=2/(1-|c|^2)>2=Tr(I) for 0<|c|<1 (checked: 2.198, 3.125, 5.556) so no two-element unambiguous POVM; adding P_?=I-P_psi-P_phi with weights 1/(1+|c|) restores a valid POVM. question: For the unambiguous-discrimination POVM with P_psi = (1/(1+|c|)) |phi_perp><phi_perp|, P_phi = (1/(1+|c|)) |psi_perp><psi_perp|, P_? = I - P_psi - P_phi, where c = <psi|phi>, |c| < 1, and |psi_perp>, |phi_perp> are defined as in the text, prove the three properties that make it a legitimate unambiguous POVM for state discrimination: (i) P_psi, P_phi, P_? are all positive semidefinite; (ii) P_psi + P_phi + P_? = I; (iii) the conclusive outcomes are unambiguous, i.e. <phi|P_psi|phi> = 0 and <psi|P_phi|psi> = 0. reference_answer: Property (ii) is immediate from the definition P_? := I - P_psi - P_phi, so P_psi + P_phi + P_? = I exactly, with no assumption on c. Property (iii): compute <phi|phi_perp>. Since |phi_perp> = (|psi> - c*|phi>)/sqrt(1-|c|^2), we get <phi|phi_perp> = (<phi|psi> - c*<phi|phi>)/sqrt(1-|c|^2) = (c* - c*)/sqrt(1-|c|^2) = 0 (using <phi|psi> = c* and <phi|phi>=1). Hence <phi|P_psi|phi> = (1/(1+|c|))|<phi|phi_perp>|^2 = 0. Symmetrically, <psi|psi_perp> = (<psi|phi> - c<psi|psi>)/sqrt(1-|c|^2) = (c - c)/sqrt(1-|c|^2) = 0, so <psi|P_phi|psi> = 0. The conclusive outcomes never fire on the wrong state. Property (i): P_psi, P_phi are nonnegative multiples of rank-one projectors |phi_perp><phi_perp|, |psi_perp><psi_perp|, hence PSD. For P_?, restrict to span{|psi>,|phi>} (off this plane I - P_psi - P_phi acts as the identity, which is PSD). Both |phi_perp> and |psi_perp> are unit vectors; a direct computation of their overlap gives |<phi_perp|psi_perp>| = |c|. In the (non-orthogonal) spanning pair {|phi_perp>, |psi_perp>}, the operator S := P_psi + P_phi = (1/(1+|c|))(|phi_perp><phi_perp| + |psi_perp><psi_perp|) is a scaled sum of two unit rank-one projectors with Gram overlap |c|; such a sum has eigenvalues (1 +/- |c|) times the scalar 1/(1+|c|), i.e. eigenvalues 1 and (1-|c|)/(1+|c|). Hence ||S|| = 1 (attained) and the smaller eigenvalue is (1-|c|)/(1+|c|) >= 0. Therefore P_? = I - S has eigenvalues 1 - 1 = 0 and 1 - (1-|c|)/(1+|c|) = 2|c|/(1+|c|), both >= 0 for |c| in [0,1). So P_? >= 0 (with a zero eigenvalue, showing the weight 1/(1+|c|) is the largest that keeps P_? PSD). All three properties hold, so the family is a valid unambiguous-discrimination POVM.

question: Lemma 9.15 assumes that for every outcome i the block encoding U_i of sqrt(P_i) uses the SAME ancilla size a and the SAME subnormalization factor beta. Investigate what breaks if these two uniformity assumptions are dropped. Specifically: (a) if the U_i had different subnormalization factors beta_i, show that the controlled unitary W = sum_i |i><i| tensor U_i followed by postselection on 0^a would NOT yield the clean superposition sum_i |i> sqrt(P_i)|psi> that is needed, and identify what spurious operator appears instead; (b) if the U_i used different ancilla registers (different sizes a_i, or disjoint ancillas), explain why a single joint postselection event '0^a' is no longer well defined and how this changes the success-probability bookkeeping. In each case state the minimal fix (if any) that restores the construction.
reference_answer: (a) Different beta_i. The block-encoding action becomes U_i |0^a>|psi> = (1/beta_i) |0^a> sqrt(P_i)|psi> + |perp_i>. After W on the uniform superposition and postselection on 0^a, the surviving (unnormalized) joint state is (1/sqrt(2^m)) sum_i (1/beta_i) |i> sqrt(P_i)|psi>. This is NOT proportional to the required sum_i |i> sqrt(P_i)|psi>: the weights are distorted by the factors 1/beta_i. Measuring the output register then yields label i with probability proportional to (1/beta_i^2) <psi|P_i|psi> rather than <psi|P_i|psi>, i.e. the effective implemented family is {P_i' = P_i/beta_i^2} (up to normalization), a DIFFERENT and generally non-complete measurement because sum_i P_i/beta_i^2 != I in general. The spurious object is a diagonal reweighting by 1/beta_i^2; statistics are biased toward outcomes with small beta_i. Minimal fix: rescale to a common beta := max_i beta_i by replacing each U_i with a block encoding of (beta_i/beta) sqrt(P_i) (pad the subnormalization up), or equivalently prepare the output register in a NON-uniform superposition sum_i (beta_i/beta)|i> designed to cancel the 1/beta_i weights, restoring sum_i |i> sqrt(P_i)|psi> after postselection. The uniform-superposition PREP and the common beta are two sides of the same requirement. (b) Different ancillas. If U_i acts on its own ancilla register of size a_i (or on disjoint physical ancillas), then 'measure the ancilla and postselect on 0^a' is ambiguous: there is no single shared register whose value 0^a flags success for every branch simultaneously. In W = sum_i |i><i| tensor U_i, branch i touches ancilla-set i while leaving the others idle, so a global postselection onto all-zeros across the union of ancillas conflates 'U_i produced its clean block' with 'the idle ancillas of the other branches happen to read 0', double counting and breaking the clean identity (I tensor <0^a| tensor I)|perp> = 0 that was essential. The bookkeeping P(succ) = (1/(beta^2 2^m)) sum_i <psi|P_i|psi> relied on a single projector |0^a><0^a| commuting with the branch structure; with per-branch ancillas the projector factorizes differently per branch and the sum no longer collapses by completeness. Minimal fix: use one shared ancilla register of common size a = max_i a_i, embedding each U_i so that it only returns the designated register to 0^a on its clean block (pad smaller encodings with unused-but-reset ancilla qubits), which is exactly the 'same ancilla size a' hypothesis. There is no cheaper fix that avoids a shared success flag: without it the postselection event is not a single projector and the completeness collapse fails.

question: Given a real matrix A with ||A||_max < 1 and A_ij real, suppose we have a bit oracle that writes a d'-bit fixed-point representation of A_ij into a work register: O~_A |0^{d'}>|i>|j> = |A~_ij>|i>|j>. Using classical arithmetic one first produces O'_A |0^d>|i>|j> = |theta~_ij>|i>|j> with theta~_ij = arccos(A_ij)/pi in [0,1) a d-bit value. Then a controlled rotation CR transfers theta~_ij to the amplitude of a fresh ancilla qubit. Prove that the full procedure O_A = (I_1 tensor (O'_A)^{-1}) * CR * (I_1 tensor O'_A), acting on |0>|0^d>|i>|j>, produces exactly the amplitude-oracle state (A~_ij |0> + sqrt(1 - A~_ij^2) |1>) |0^d>|i>|j>, i.e. with the d-bit work register returned to |0^d>. State precisely why the final uncomputation step (O'_A)^{-1} is mandatory -- i.e. why the work register cannot simply be discarded ('no free cleanup') -- and what would go wrong with the amplitude oracle's action if it were left entangled.
reference_answer: Track the registers (ancilla qubit, d-bit work register, index registers i,j). Step 1 (apply I_1 tensor O'_A): |0>|0^d>|i>|j> -> |0>|theta~_ij>|i>|j>. The index registers are untouched; the work register now holds the angle. Step 2 (controlled rotation CR, controlled on the work register, acting on the ancilla qubit): CR implements |0>|theta~> -> (cos(pi theta~)|0> + sin(pi theta~)|1>)|theta~>. With A~_ij := cos(pi theta~_ij) (and theta~_ij = arccos(A_ij)/pi so cos(pi theta~_ij) = A_ij up to the d-bit rounding), this gives (A~_ij |0> + sqrt(1 - A~_ij^2) |1>) |theta~_ij>|i>|j>, using sin(pi theta~) = sqrt(1 - cos^2(pi theta~)) = sqrt(1 - A~_ij^2) >= 0 for theta~ in [0,1) (nonnegative sine on (0,pi)). Step 3 (apply I_1 tensor (O'_A)^{-1}): the rotation acted only on the ancilla qubit and did NOT alter the work register, so (O'_A)^{-1} maps |theta~_ij>|i>|j> back to |0^d>|i>|j> conditioned on each (i,j). Crucially (O'_A)^{-1} is a function only of (i,j), which are unchanged, so it uncomputes the angle coherently and uniformly across the ancilla's |0> and |1> branches (it acts as identity on the ancilla qubit). The result is (A~_ij |0> + sqrt(1 - A~_ij^2) |1>) |0^d>|i>|j>, exactly the amplitude oracle O_A with the work register restored. Why uncomputation is mandatory (no free cleanup): if we skipped (O'_A)^{-1} and merely 'discarded' |theta~_ij>, the true quantum state is (A~_ij|0> + sqrt(1-A~_ij^2)|1>) |theta~_ij>|i>|j> -- the ancilla qubit is correlated with the work register through the shared dependence on (i,j). Tracing out (discarding) the work register leaves a MIXED state on the ancilla+index registers whenever different (i,j) produce different theta~, destroying the coherent superposition A~_ij|0> + sqrt(1-A~_ij^2)|1>. Worse, when O_A is used inside a larger block-encoding circuit that interferes different (i,j) branches (e.g. the sparse-matrix LCU of Fig. 9.7), the residual record |theta~_ij> acts as a which-path marker: branches with different angles no longer interfere, so the intended matrix element <0|<i|U_A|0>|j> = A_ij is corrupted into a decohered, generally wrong value. Hence the garbage register must be coherently returned to |0^d> by (O'_A)^{-1}; discarding is not free because a quantum computer cannot erase an entangled register without either uncomputation or decoherence. The ancilla qubit carrying the amplitude is deliberately NOT uncomputed -- it is the output -- but the intermediate angle register must be.

reviews.notes: Example 9.16, verified vs Eq.(9.70)-(9.71): O'_A loads |theta~_ij>; CR gives (cos(pi theta~)|0>+sin(pi theta~)|1>)|theta~> with sin>=0 on range and A~_ij=cos(pi theta~); (O'_A)^{-1} depends only on unchanged (i,j), acts as identity on the ancilla, so it uncomputes |theta~> coherently across both ancilla branches. Decoherence/which-path argument correct: discarding the entangled work register would leave a marker that kills (i,j)-branch interference downstream, so the final inverse query is mandatory - matches source emphasis on uncomputation. Faithful, original phrasing.

question: The amplitude oracle O_A |0>|i>|j> = (A_ij |0> + sqrt(1 - |A_ij|^2) |1>) |i>|j> is often introduced alongside a standing convenience assumption ||A||_max < 1. Determine the EXACT condition under which the right-hand side is a valid normalized state and the oracle is a legitimate unitary action, by analyzing the three regimes |A_ij| < 1, |A_ij| = 1, and |A_ij| > 1 (for each: is it a unit vector, what does the controlled-rotation angle do, does the oracle exist). Then state carefully whether the strict inequality ||A||_max < 1 is NECESSARY or merely a sufficient convenience, explain the downstream consequence for the subnormalization factor of the resulting block encoding, and why one preprocesses A by dividing out an upper bound on ||A||_max before building the oracle.
reference_answer: The right-hand side A_ij|0> + sqrt(1-|A_ij|^2)|1> is a unit vector with a real nonnegative second coefficient iff 1 - |A_ij|^2 >= 0, i.e. iff |A_ij| <= 1. The sharp validity condition is therefore |A_ij| <= 1, NOT the strict |A_ij| < 1. Regime |A_ij| < 1: 1 - |A_ij|^2 > 0, the state is a genuine normalized superposition with rotation angle theta = 2 arccos(|A_ij|) strictly in (0,pi); the amplitude of |0> faithfully encodes A_ij with both branches populated. Regime |A_ij| = 1: 1 - |A_ij|^2 = 0, so the second (sqrt) term is exactly zero and the state is A_ij|0> (a unit vector, basis state up to phase). This is a perfectly LEGITIMATE normalized amplitude oracle -- the rotation angle is simply 0 or pi (an endpoint of the range), and O_A remains a valid unitary action; nothing degenerates about its validity. The only caveat is purely numerical: if finite-precision arithmetic rounds A~_ij slightly ABOVE 1, then sqrt(1-A~_ij^2) becomes imaginary, so one keeps a small guard below 1 for robustness. But |A_ij| = 1 itself is inside the valid regime. Regime |A_ij| > 1: now 1 - |A_ij|^2 < 0 and sqrt(1 - |A_ij|^2) is imaginary, so there is no real controlled-rotation producing A_ij|0> + sqrt(1-|A_ij|^2)|1> as a unit vector; the amplitude oracle of this form does not exist. An entry of magnitude strictly above 1 cannot be encoded as a single-qubit amplitude. Necessity vs sufficiency: the oracle exists and is normalized for the full closed range |A_ij| <= 1, so ||A||_max <= 1 (allowing equality) is the actual requirement. The strict ||A||_max < 1 commonly assumed in the text is a SUFFICIENT CONVENIENCE, not a necessity: it guarantees a non-degenerate two-branch rotation for every entry and a numerical margin against rounding above 1, but entries exactly equal to 1 are still fine. It is only |A_ij| > 1 that is genuinely excluded. Downstream: a block encoding built from the oracle has subnormalization factor at least ||A|| (for the s-sparse LCU construction exactly alpha = s ||A||_max). If some |A_ij| > 1 the per-entry amplitude encoding is impossible; and even in the valid regime a larger ||A||_max pushes alpha up. Therefore one preprocesses by choosing a known upper bound M >= ||A||_max and building the oracle for A/M, whose entries satisfy |(A/M)_ij| <= 1, guaranteeing valid normalized states and a controlled subnormalization; taking M strictly above ||A||_max additionally restores the strict-inequality numerical margin.

question: Two input models for the entries of a matrix A appear in the sparse block-encoding discussion: the BIT oracle O~_A |0^{d'}>|i>|j> = |A~_ij>|i>|j>, which writes a classical fixed-point string into a register, and the AMPLITUDE oracle O_A |0>|i>|j> = (A_ij|0> + sqrt(1-|A_ij|^2)|1>)|i>|j>, which encodes the entry as the amplitude of an ancilla qubit. Explain conceptually (i) what distinguishes the two as computational resources -- which is a 'digital/query' interface and which is an 'analog/amplitude' interface; (ii) why building the amplitude oracle from the bit oracle requires both controlled rotations (gate work) and uncomputation (query work), i.e. the amplitude oracle is strictly derived, not primitive; and (iii) in a resource count for the overall block encoding, why it is natural to charge the construction one forward and one inverse bit-oracle query plus the gates of a controlled rotation, and why the work register must be counted as borrowed (returned clean), not consumed.
reference_answer: (i) The bit oracle is a DIGITAL/query interface: it deposits a classical bit string A~_ij into a register, which can be read, fanned out via CNOTs, and processed by reversible arithmetic. It makes the numeric value explicitly available but says nothing by itself about amplitudes. The amplitude oracle is an ANALOG/amplitude interface: it hides the value A_ij in the probability amplitude of |0> on an ancilla qubit, which is exactly the form a block encoding needs (the encoded entry must appear as an <0|...|0>-type amplitude), but which cannot be read out directly without measurement/estimation. The two interfaces trade explicitness (bit) for direct usability inside interference-based circuits (amplitude). (ii) The amplitude oracle is derived, not primitive: to turn a stored value into an amplitude one must (a) convert A~_ij to an angle theta~_ij via reversible classical arithmetic (a bit-oracle-type query O'_A), (b) perform a controlled Y-rotation CR that maps the angle into the ancilla amplitude -- irreducibly gate work, since no bit oracle produces amplitudes on its own -- and (c) uncompute the angle register with (O'_A)^{-1}, a second (inverse) query, to disentangle the amplitude qubit from the intermediate data. Thus amplitude oracle = query + controlled-rotation gates + inverse query. The rotation is where 'digital' becomes 'analog'; the two queries bracket it to keep the transformation reversible. (iii) Resource accounting: the natural charge is one forward bit-oracle query O'_A, the controlled-rotation gate(s) CR (whose gate count grows with the angle precision d), and one inverse query (O'_A)^{-1}. Both the forward and inverse queries are counted because reversibility forces the uncomputation; you cannot amortize it away. The d-bit work register is counted as BORROWED/clean ancilla: it starts in |0^d> and must be returned to |0^d> by the uncomputation, so it does not add to the persistent ancilla budget of the block encoding (it is reusable across calls), but it is NOT free either -- it must physically exist during the call and the inverse query must be paid for. Counting it as consumed would overstate the ancilla footprint; counting the uncomputation as free would understate the query/gate cost. The honest ledger is: +2 queries, +CR gates, +d borrowed-and-returned work qubits, +1 persistent amplitude ancilla (the actual output qubit), with 'no free cleanup' meaning the inverse query is a real line item.

question: Let A be a diagonal N x N matrix (a 1-sparse matrix whose only nonzero entries are A_ii), with ||A||_max <= 1. Using the simplified amplitude oracle O_A |0>|i> = (A_ii |0> + sqrt(1 - |A_ii|^2) |1>) |i>, set U_A := O_A. Prove by direct evaluation of the matrix element <0|<i| U_A |0>|j> that U_A is a (1,1)-block-encoding of A, i.e. <0|<i| U_A |0>|j> = A_ii delta_ij, so THIS construction has subnormalization factor alpha = 1 with a single ancilla qubit. Explain why no index-permutation oracle is needed here, in contrast to the general 1-sparse case. Then discuss precisely in what sense alpha = 1 is or is not optimal: state the general lower bound any block encoding must obey, and say whether alpha = 1 is a global optimum for every diagonal A with ||A||_max <= 1 or only in a specific case.
reference_answer: Apply U_A = O_A to |0>|j>: U_A |0>|j> = (A_jj |0> + sqrt(1-|A_jj|^2)|1>)|j>. Now take the overlap with <0|<i|: <0|<i| U_A |0>|j> = A_jj <0|0> <i|j> + sqrt(1-|A_jj|^2) <0|1> <i|j>. The second term vanishes because <0|1> = 0. The first term is A_jj <i|j> = A_jj delta_ij. When i = j this equals A_jj = A_ii; when i != j it is 0. Hence <0|<i| U_A |0>|j> = A_ii delta_ij, which is precisely the (i,j) entry of the diagonal matrix A. By the definition of block encoding, (<0| tensor I) U_A (|0> tensor I) = A exactly, with one ancilla qubit (m = 1) and subnormalization alpha = 1, so U_A is in BE_{1,1}(A). No permutation oracle is needed because for a DIAGONAL matrix the row index equals the column index: the single nonzero entry in column j sits at row c(j) = j, i.e. the sparsity permutation c is the identity. In the general 1-sparse case the unique nonzero entry of column j lives at row c(j) != j, so one must apply an index permutation O_c |j> = |c(j)> to move the amplitude-carrying basis state from |j> to |c(j)>; for the diagonal case c = id, so O_c = I and U_A = O_A alone suffices. Optimality -- stated carefully. The general lower bound is that any (alpha,m)-block-encoding of A must satisfy alpha >= ||A|| (operator norm), because the encoded top-left block equals A/alpha and a sub-block of a unitary has operator norm at most 1, forcing ||A||/alpha <= 1. For a diagonal A, ||A|| = max_i |A_ii|. The present construction FIXES alpha = 1 regardless of the entries; this value saturates the lower bound (hence is globally optimal) ONLY in the case ||A|| = max_i |A_ii| = 1, e.g. when some |A_ii| = 1. If instead max_i |A_ii| = r < 1 strictly, then alpha = 1 is a VALID but NOT optimal subnormalization: the lower bound only demands alpha >= r, and a smaller alpha = r is mathematically achievable -- for example by encoding A/r (whose max entry has modulus 1) with this very construction to obtain an (r,1)-block-encoding of A. Thus alpha = 1 is a property of THIS fixed construction, globally optimal exactly when ||A|| = 1, and for ||A|| < 1 merely a valid upper bound rather than the minimum. The honest statement: the construction yields alpha = 1; it meets the alpha >= ||A|| floor iff ||A|| = 1, and is not subnormalization-optimal when ||A|| < 1.

reviews.notes: Example 9.17 (Eq.9.72-9.73). The core (1,1)-block-encoding identity <0|<i|O_A|0>|j>=A_ii delta_ij is CORRECT and holds for ALL diagonal A with ||A||_max<=1, INCLUDING A=0 (both sides 0); c(j)=j triviality (no O_c) correct; the earlier coordinator-flagged false GLOBAL-optimality claim (alpha=1 optimal for every A) WAS fixed by the author (reference/rubric r4/step4/native_nl now say alpha>=||A||=max_i|A_ii|, alpha=1 saturates iff ||A||=1, and for ||A||<1 a smaller alpha=||A|| is achievable). HOWEVER a residual EDGE-CASE OVERCLAIM remains and is why this item is PENDING: the 'smaller alpha=||A|| achievable, e.g. by encoding A/||A||' statement FAILS at the zero matrix A=0, which is in the stated domain (||A||_max=0<=1): 'A/||A||' is division by zero/undefined, and a subnormalization must be strictly positive (the infimum of valid alpha for A=0 is 0 but UNATTAINED, so there is no achievable minimal alpha=||A||=0). The graded identity portion is unaffected; only the optimality discussion needs the qualifier.

question: To block-encode a general s-sparse matrix A (at most s nonzeros per row and per column, ||A||_max = 1), one decomposes A into 1-sparse pieces. View the sparsity pattern as a bipartite graph with left vertices the row indices and right vertices the column indices, with an edge (i,j) whenever A_ij != 0; pad with zero entries so every row and column has exactly s incident edges, making the graph s-regular. Prove that this s-regular bipartite graph decomposes into exactly s disjoint perfect matchings, so that A = sum_{ell in [s]} A^{(ell)} with each A^{(ell)} 1-sparse, and explain how each matching ell yields a permutation j -> c(j,ell) of [N] that can be queried by a single permutation oracle O_c |ell>|j> = |ell>|c(j,ell)>. Then explain why this is precisely what makes the LCU circuit of Fig. 9.7 produce a block encoding with subnormalization factor alpha = s, and why alpha = s (= s ||A||_max) is the natural choice rather than something smaller.
reference_answer: Edge decomposition: an s-regular bipartite graph has, by Koenig's line-coloring theorem (edge-coloring version), chromatic index exactly s, i.e. its edges can be properly colored with s colors so that no two edges of the same color share a vertex. Each color class is therefore a set of vertex-disjoint edges covering -- because the graph is s-regular and bipartite with equal side sizes N -- every vertex exactly once; that is a PERFECT MATCHING. There are exactly s color classes, so the edge set partitions into s disjoint perfect matchings M_1,...,M_s. From matchings to permutations: fix matching ell. In a perfect matching every column vertex j is matched to a unique row vertex, call it c(j,ell); conversely every row is matched to a unique column. Hence j -> c(j,ell) is a bijection of [N] onto itself, i.e. a permutation. Packaging all s matchings, the single oracle O_c |ell>|j> = |ell>|c(j,ell)> encodes, for each color ell, the corresponding permutation. 1-sparse pieces: define A^{(ell)} by A^{(ell)}_{c(j,ell),j} = A_{c(j,ell),j} and all other entries zero. Each A^{(ell)} has exactly one nonzero per row and per column (it is supported on matching M_ell), so it is 1-sparse; and because the s matchings partition ALL edges of the (padded) graph, every nonzero entry A_ij belongs to exactly one matching, giving A = sum_{ell in [s]} A^{(ell)}. LCU and alpha = s: the circuit uses the s-qubit Hadamard-type map D |0^s> = (1/sqrt(s)) sum_ell |ell> to form a uniform superposition over the s matchings, O_A to load the entry amplitude for the selected matching, and O_c to route the index; this is an LCU over the equal-weight family {A^{(ell)}} with s terms each of 1-norm (coefficient) at most ||A||_max = 1. The standard LCU block-encoding subnormalization is the coefficient 1-norm, here sum_ell 1 = s. So U_A in BE_{s, s+1}(A), i.e. <0|<0^s|<i| U_A |0>|0^s>|j> = (1/s) A_ij, matching alpha = s. Why alpha = s is natural: Lemma 2.46 gives ||A|| <= s ||A||_max, and any block encoding must satisfy alpha >= ||A||, which for a worst-case s-sparse matrix can be as large as s ||A||_max; the construction attains alpha = s ||A||_max = s, so it meets the generic sparse bound. One cannot generally pick alpha < s with this oracle structure because the equal 1/sqrt(s) amplitudes spread the single real entry over s branches, giving exactly a 1/s matrix element; a smaller alpha would require either knowing the entries are smaller (reducing ||A||_max) or using a non-uniform PREP tailored to the actual row/column norms.

question: Consider the s-sparse LCU block-encoding circuit U_A = (I tensor D tensor I)(I tensor O_c) O_A (I tensor D tensor I), where D |0^s> = (1/sqrt(s)) sum_{ell in [s]} |ell>, O_A |0>|ell>|j> = (A_{c(j,ell),j}|0> + sqrt(1 - |A_{c(j,ell),j}|^2)|1>)|ell>|j>, and O_c |ell>|j> = |ell>|c(j,ell)>, with each j -> c(j,ell) a permutation. By propagating |0>|0^s>|j> through D, O_A, O_c and separately propagating |0>|0^s>|i> through D (using that D is Hermitian), evaluate the inner product <0|<0^s|<i| U_A |0>|0^s>|j> and show it equals (1/s) A_ij. Explain carefully why the single clean sum over ell collapses to one surviving term and how the Kronecker delta delta_{i,c(j,ell)} selects it; also explain why the |1> (unflagged) component of O_A does not contribute.
reference_answer: Forward propagation of the source |0>|0^s>|j>: Apply D to the s-qubit register: |0>|0^s>|j> -> (1/sqrt(s)) sum_ell |0>|ell>|j>. Apply O_A: -> (1/sqrt(s)) sum_ell (A_{c(j,ell),j}|0> + sqrt(1-|A_{c(j,ell),j}|^2)|1>)|ell>|j>. Apply O_c (permuting the index register): -> (1/sqrt(s)) sum_ell (A_{c(j,ell),j}|0> + sqrt(1-|...|^2)|1>)|ell>|c(j,ell)>. Backward propagation of the target: instead of multiplying the leftmost (I tensor D tensor I) onto this line, apply it to |0>|0^s>|i>; since D is Hermitian, (I tensor D tensor I) on the left acts as D on |0^s> on the right of the bra, giving the ket (1/sqrt(s)) sum_{ell'} |0>|ell'>|i>. Inner product: <0|<0^s|<i| U_A |0>|0^s>|j> = ((1/sqrt(s)) sum_{ell'} <0|<ell'|<i|) ((1/sqrt(s)) sum_ell (A_{c(j,ell),j}|0> + sqrt(1-|...|^2)|1>)|ell>|c(j,ell)>). The ancilla overlap <0 | (A|0> + sqrt(...)|1>) = A_{c(j,ell),j}, because <0|0> = 1 and <0|1> = 0 -- this is exactly why the |1> component drops out: the success flag <0| annihilates it. The s-register overlap <ell'|ell> = delta_{ell',ell} collapses the double sum to a single sum over ell. The index overlap <i|c(j,ell)> = delta_{i,c(j,ell)} keeps only the matching(s) ell for which c(j,ell) = i, i.e. the row that column j is matched to in matching ell equals the queried row i. Thus <0|<0^s|<i| U_A |0>|0^s>|j> = (1/s) sum_ell A_{c(j,ell),j} delta_{i,c(j,ell)} = (1/s) A_ij: if A_ij != 0 there is a unique ell with c(j,ell) = i (that nonzero entry lives in exactly one matching), contributing A_{i,j}; if A_ij = 0 no ell satisfies both the delta and a nonzero entry, so the sum is 0. The overall (1/s) is the LCU subnormalization. Hence U_A in BE_{s,s+1}(A).

question: An alternative s-sparse input model uses two (2n)-qubit oracles O_r |ell>|i> = |r(i,ell)>|i> and O_c |ell>|j> = |c(j,ell)>|j>, where r(i,ell) and c(j,ell) give the ell-th nonzero entry in row i and column j respectively, together with the entry oracle O_A |0>|i>|j> = (A_ij|0> + sqrt(1-|A_ij|^2)|1>)|i>|j> (controlled by both indices). The circuit of Fig. 9.8 applies D, O_c, O_A, then a SWAP, then D and O_r. Prove that the resulting U_A satisfies <0|<0^n|<i| U_A |0>|0^n|j> = (1/s) A_ij, so U_A in BE_{s,n+1}(A). In particular, explain the roles of the two separate delta constraints delta_{i,c(j,ell)} and delta_{r(i,ell'),j}, and why -- when A_ij = 0 -- the computation still gives 0 even though the rotation in O_A may be arbitrary on zero entries.
reference_answer: Propagate the source |0>|0^n>|j>. Apply D, O_c, O_A: |0>|0^n>|j> -> (1/sqrt(s)) sum_ell (A_{c(j,ell),j}|0> + sqrt(1-|A_{c(j,ell),j}|^2)|1>)|c(j,ell)>|j>, where O_c has written the matched row index c(j,ell) into the first register and O_A loaded the entry amplitude (controlled by the row c(j,ell) and column j). Apply SWAP, which exchanges the (row-like) and (column-like) registers: -> (1/sqrt(s)) sum_ell (A_{c(j,ell),j}|0> + sqrt(1-|...|^2)|1>)|j>|c(j,ell)>. Propagate the target |0>|0^n>|i>. Apply D and O_r: -> (1/sqrt(s)) sum_{ell'} |0>|r(i,ell')>|i>. Inner product: <0|<0^n|<i| U_A |0>|0^n>|j> = (1/s) sum_{ell,ell'} A_{c(j,ell),j} <r(i,ell')|j> <i|c(j,ell)> (the ancilla <0| picks out A and kills the sqrt(1-|.|^2)|1> term). The two deltas: <i|c(j,ell)> = delta_{i,c(j,ell)} forces the matched row of column j in matching ell to be exactly i; <r(i,ell')|j> = delta_{r(i,ell'),j} forces the matched column of row i in matching ell' to be exactly j. Evaluate: = (1/s) sum_{ell,ell'} A_{c(j,ell),j} delta_{i,c(j,ell)} delta_{r(i,ell'),j}. If A_ij != 0, there is a unique ell with c(j,ell) = i (the nonzero (i,j) lies in exactly one column-matching) and a unique ell' with r(i,ell') = j (likewise for the row structure), so exactly one term survives, giving (1/s) A_{i,j} = (1/s) A_ij. If A_ij = 0: there is NO matching ell with c(j,ell) = i that carries a nonzero entry, and/or no ell' with r(i,ell') = j; hence for every (ell,ell') at least one delta is zero OR the surviving A_{c(j,ell),j} with c(j,ell) = i equals A_ij = 0. Either way the sum is 0. Crucially, even though O_A's rotation on a zero entry may be arbitrary (the text allows this), that arbitrary amplitude never contributes to the final matrix element: the two independent deltas from O_c and O_r only let a term survive when BOTH the column structure routes column j to row i and the row structure routes row i to column j, which happens only on genuine nonzero positions; on zero positions the position is simply not in the sparsity pattern so no (ell,ell') pair selects it. The joint row/column consistency is what makes the arbitrary zero-entry rotations harmless. Thus <0|<0^n|<i| U_A |0>|0^n>|j> = (1/s) A_ij and U_A in BE_{s,n+1}(A).
