question: A Hermitian matrix A does NOT automatically have a Hermitian block encoding: even for a Hermitian diagonal A and even when the approximation error is exactly 0, a generic (alpha, m, 0)-block-encoding U_A need not satisfy U_A = U_A^dagger -- only the upper-left n-qubit block of U_A is guaranteed Hermitian. (i) Explain precisely what the block-encoding definition does and does not constrain about U_A, so that Hermiticity of the encoded block does not propagate to the whole unitary. (ii) Give a concrete small example illustrating that the amplitude-oracle block encoding of a Hermitian diagonal matrix (Example 9.17) is generally not a Hermitian matrix. (iii) State what additional structural requirement defines a Hermitian block encoding (Definition 9.23) and why it is a strictly stronger condition useful for qubitization.
reference_answer: (i) The block-encoding definition only constrains the top-left n-qubit block: U_A in BE_{alpha,m}(A, 0) means (<0^m| tensor I) U_A (|0^m> tensor I) = A/alpha, i.e. it pins down the single sub-block indexed by ancilla = 0^m on both input and output. The remaining blocks (ancilla going 0^m -> nonzero, nonzero -> 0^m, and nonzero -> nonzero) are completely free apart from the global constraint that U_A be unitary. Hermiticity of A forces the top-left block to be Hermitian, but says nothing about the off-diagonal blocks or the complementary block; unitarity does not force those to make U_A self-adjoint. So A = A^dagger does not imply U_A = U_A^dagger. (ii) Example: take the 1x1-ancilla amplitude oracle for a diagonal A with a single real entry a = A_11 in (0,1). On the relevant 2x2 ancilla block (fixed index), U_A acts as the single-qubit rotation R = [[a, -sqrt(1-a^2)],[sqrt(1-a^2), a]] (a real rotation by angle theta with cos theta = a). This R is NOT symmetric/Hermitian: its off-diagonal entries are -sqrt(1-a^2) and +sqrt(1-a^2), which differ in sign, so R != R^T = R^dagger (for real R). The top-left entry is a = A_11 (Hermitian, trivially), yet the full U_A (a rotation, not a reflection) is not Hermitian. Thus even the block encoding of a Hermitian (indeed diagonal) matrix is generically non-Hermitian. (iii) Definition 9.23 adds the explicit requirement U_A = U_A^dagger: an (alpha,m,eps)-block-encoding that is ALSO a Hermitian matrix is called an (alpha,m,eps)-Hermitian-block-encoding (set HBE_{alpha,m}(A,eps)). This is strictly stronger: it is an extra global constraint on all blocks of U_A, not just the encoded sub-block, and generic block encodings (like the rotation above) violate it. It is useful for qubitization because when U_A = U_A^dagger each eigenvector |v_i> of A is 'qubitized' into a 2D invariant subspace H_i on which U_A acts as a reflection [[lambda_i, sqrt(1-lambda_i^2)],[sqrt(1-lambda_i^2), -lambda_i]]; the self-adjointness is exactly what lets you apply U_A a second time to Eq. (9.30) and close the 2D subspace (Eq. (9.34)), which is the mechanism that turns U_A Z_Pi into a rotation implementing Chebyshev polynomials T_k(A). Without Hermiticity the simple reflection structure (and hence the clean two-step closure) is not available.

question: For an s-sparse Hermitian matrix A with ||A||_max <= 1, the Hermitian block-encoding circuit of Fig. 9.9 uses one location oracle O_c |ell>|j> = |c(j,ell)>|j>, an (n+1)-qubit SWAP, and a square-root entry oracle O_A |i>|0>|j> = |i>(sqrt(A_ij)|0> + sqrt(1 - |A_ij|)|1>)|j> acting on a single-qubit register, where for complex/negative entries one writes A_ij = |A_ij| e^{i theta_ij} and sqrt(A_ij) = sqrt(|A_ij|) e^{i theta_ij / 2}. Prove that the circuit yields <0|<0^n|<0|<i| U_A |0>|0^n>|0>|j> = (1/s) A_ij, so U_A in HBE_{s,n+2}(A). You must show explicitly where Hermiticity A_ij = A_ji^* is used to combine the two square-root factors sqrt(A_{c(j,ell),j}) and sqrt(A_{c(i,ell'),i})^* into A_ij.
reference_answer: Propagate the source |0>|0^n>|0>|j> through D, O_c, O_A: -> (1/sqrt(s)) sum_ell |0>|c(j,ell)>(sqrt(A_{c(j,ell),j})|0> + sqrt(1-|A_{c(j,ell),j}|)|1>)|j>. Apply the (n+1)-qubit SWAP, which exchanges the first register pair (a,i) with the second (b,j): -> (1/sqrt(s)) sum_ell (sqrt(A_{c(j,ell),j})|0> + sqrt(1-|...|)|1>)|j>|0>|c(j,ell)>. Propagate the target |0>|0^n>|0>|i> through D, O_c, O_A: -> (1/sqrt(s)) sum_{ell'} |0>|c(i,ell')>(sqrt(A_{c(i,ell'),i})|0> + sqrt(1-|A_{c(i,ell'),i}|)|1>)|i>. Form the inner product <0|<0^n|<0|<i| U_A |0>|0^n>|0>|j>. The two single-qubit ancillas each contribute a <0|(sqrt(A)|0> + sqrt(1-|A|)|1>) overlap, keeping only the sqrt(A)|0> part (the |1> terms are annihilated by <0|): one factor sqrt(A_{c(j,ell),j}) from the source and, from the target bra, the conjugate sqrt(A_{c(i,ell'),i})^* (a bra conjugates amplitudes). The register overlaps give delta_{i,c(j,ell)} (target row index i must match the routed source index c(j,ell)) and delta_{c(i,ell'),j} (routed target index must match j). So <0|<0^n|<0|<i| U_A |0>|0^n>|0>|j> = (1/s) sum_{ell,ell'} sqrt(A_{c(j,ell),j}) sqrt(A_{c(i,ell'),i})^* delta_{i,c(j,ell)} delta_{c(i,ell'),j}. When A_ij != 0 there is a unique ell with c(j,ell) = i and a unique ell' with c(i,ell') = j, so the surviving term is (1/s) sqrt(A_{i,j}) sqrt(A_{j,i})^*. Now use Hermiticity: A_ji = A_ij^*, hence sqrt(A_{j,i})^* = sqrt(A_ij^*)^* = sqrt(A_ij) (since conjugating the entry and then its square root returns the original square root: (sqrt(|A_ij|) e^{-i theta_ij/2})^* = sqrt(|A_ij|) e^{i theta_ij/2} = sqrt(A_ij)). Therefore sqrt(A_ij) sqrt(A_ji)^* = sqrt(A_ij) sqrt(A_ij) = (sqrt(A_ij))^2 = A_ij. This gives (1/s) A_ij, and when A_ij = 0 the deltas select no nonzero term, giving 0. Hence <0|<0^n|<0|<i| U_A |0>|0^n>|0>|j> = (1/s) A_ij for all i,j, so U_A in HBE_{s,n+2}(A). The two-register symmetric structure (source and target each run D, O_c, O_A, bridged by SWAP) is what makes U_A Hermitian, and Hermiticity of A is precisely what lets the two half-entries sqrt(A_{ij}) and sqrt(A_{ji})^* multiply back to the full entry A_ij.

question: The block-encoding notion generalizes beyond computational-basis subspaces. Fix rank-N and rank-N' orthogonal projectors Pi, Pi' on an ambient space C^{MN} (M = 2^m), with orthonormal bases {|phi_j>}_{j in [N]} for range(Pi) and {|psi_i>}_{i in [N']} for range(Pi'). Collect these as the first columns of unitaries Xi, Xi' and let Xi_N, (Xi')_{N'} be those column blocks. For a unitary U_A on C^{MN}, define the induced block A~ := ((Xi')_{N'})^dagger U_A Xi_N in C^{N' x N}. Prove that the (i,j) entry of A~ equals <psi_i| U_A |phi_j>, that A~ coincides with the compression Pi' U_A Pi expressed in the chosen bases, and hence that the exact relation Pi' U_A Pi = sum_{i,j} |psi_i> A_ij <phi_j| is equivalent to A~ = A. Then state the (alpha,m,eps)-generalized block-encoding condition ||A - alpha A~|| <= eps and explain why it reduces to the ordinary computational-basis definition when Pi = Pi' = |0^m><0^m| tensor I and N' = N.
reference_answer: Entry formula: Xi_N has columns |phi_0>,...,|phi_{N-1}>, so Xi_N |e_j> = |phi_j> for the standard basis vector |e_j> of C^N; similarly (Xi')_{N'} |e_i> = |psi_i>, hence ((Xi')_{N'})^dagger |x> has i-th component <psi_i|x>. Therefore the (i,j) entry of A~ = ((Xi')_{N'})^dagger U_A Xi_N is A~_{ij} = <e_i| ((Xi')_{N'})^dagger U_A Xi_N |e_j> = (((Xi')_{N'})|e_i>)^dagger U_A (Xi_N |e_j>) = <psi_i| U_A |phi_j>. Compression identity: the orthogonal projectors can be written Pi = sum_j |phi_j><phi_j| and Pi' = sum_i |psi_i><psi_i| (spectral form on their ranges). Then Pi' U_A Pi = sum_{i,j} |psi_i> <psi_i| U_A |phi_j> <phi_j| = sum_{i,j} |psi_i> A~_{ij} <phi_j|. So Pi' U_A Pi, re-expressed in the bases {|psi_i>}, {|phi_j>}, has exactly the matrix of coefficients A~. Consequently the exact encoding requirement Pi' U_A Pi = sum_{i,j} |psi_i> A_ij <phi_j| holds if and only if A~_{ij} = A_ij for all i,j, i.e. A~ = A. Approximate condition: allowing a subnormalization alpha and error eps, U_A is an (alpha,m,eps)-generalized block-encoding of A with respect to (Pi,Pi') iff ||A - alpha A~|| <= eps (operator norm), i.e. the compression alpha A~ = alpha Pi' U_A Pi (in the chosen bases) approximates A. Reduction to the usual definition: set Pi = Pi' = Pi_{0^m} := |0^m><0^m| tensor I and N' = N. Then range(Pi) = range(Pi') is the computational ancilla-0^m subspace; choosing Xi = Xi' = I (identity, whose first N columns are |0^m>|j>) gives Xi_N |e_j> = |0^m>|j> and (Xi')_{N'} |e_i> = |0^m>|i>, so A~_{ij} = <0^m|<i| U_A |0^m>|j>, which is exactly the standard top-left block (<0^m| tensor I) U_A (|0^m> tensor I). Thus ||A - alpha A~|| <= eps becomes the ordinary (alpha,m,eps)-block-encoding condition. The generalization is purely a change of input/output subspaces (via Pi, Pi' and the basis unitaries) from the fixed computational ancilla-flag subspace to arbitrary ones.

question: For a square matrix A with SVD A = W Sigma V^dagger, three generalized matrix functions are defined: f^diamond(A) = W f(Sigma) V^dagger (balanced), f^triangleright(A) = V f(Sigma) V^dagger (right), f^triangleleft(A) = W f(Sigma) W^dagger (left). The singular value transformation uses the diamond version for odd f and the right/triangleright version for even f. Prove that when A is Hermitian with eigendecomposition A = V D V^dagger (D indefinite, real), writing the SVD as A = W Sigma V^dagger with W = V sign(D) and Sigma = |D|, the singular value transformation f_SV(A) equals the ordinary eigenvalue transformation f(A) = V f(D) V^dagger whenever f has definite parity (odd or even). Treat the odd and even cases separately, and explain why definite parity is exactly the hypothesis that removes the sign ambiguity between singular values |lambda| and eigenvalues lambda.
reference_answer: Setup: A Hermitian gives A = V D V^dagger with real diagonal D = diag(lambda_i). Its SVD is A = W Sigma V^dagger with Sigma = |D| = diag(|lambda_i|) (singular values are nonnegative) and W = V sign(D), where sign(D) = diag(sign(lambda_i)) flips the sign of the i-th column of V whenever lambda_i < 0. One checks W Sigma V^dagger = V sign(D) |D| V^dagger = V D V^dagger = A, since sign(D)|D| = D. Odd case: f_SV(A) = f^diamond(A) = W f(Sigma) V^dagger = V sign(D) f(|D|) V^dagger. Now f(|D|) = diag(f(|lambda_i|)). Because f is odd, f(|lambda_i|) = sign(lambda_i) f(lambda_i) for each i: if lambda_i >= 0 then |lambda_i| = lambda_i and sign = +1; if lambda_i < 0 then f(|lambda_i|) = f(-lambda_i) = -f(lambda_i) = sign(lambda_i) f(lambda_i). Hence sign(D) f(|D|) = diag(sign(lambda_i) * sign(lambda_i) f(lambda_i)) = diag(f(lambda_i)) = f(D) (using sign(lambda_i)^2 = 1 for lambda_i != 0). Therefore f_SV(A) = V f(D) V^dagger = f(A). Even case: f_SV(A) = f^triangleright(A) = V f(Sigma) V^dagger = V f(|D|) V^dagger. Because f is even, f(|lambda_i|) = f(lambda_i) for every i (f(-x) = f(x)), so f(|D|) = f(D). Therefore f_SV(A) = V f(D) V^dagger = f(A). Role of definite parity: the SVD only sees |lambda_i| (the singular values are the absolute eigenvalues), discarding the sign carried by eigenvalues. To reconstruct f(A) = V f(D) V^dagger one must recover f(lambda_i) from f(|lambda_i|). This is possible exactly when the sign of f(lambda_i) relative to f(|lambda_i|) is determined by the sign of lambda_i in a fixed way: for odd f the sign flips with lambda_i (and the diamond's W = V sign(D) supplies precisely that flip), while for even f there is no sign to recover (f ignores it). For an f WITHOUT definite parity, f(lambda) and f(-lambda) are independent, so f(|lambda_i|) does not determine f(lambda_i) and the SVT cannot equal the eigenvalue transformation; definite parity is thus the exact structural hypothesis that eliminates the |lambda| vs lambda sign ambiguity.

question: For a general square matrix A with SVD given by A|v_i> = sigma_i|w_i>, A^dagger|w_i> = sigma_i|v_i>, sigma_i >= 0, define the one-ancilla dilated Hermitian matrix A~ = [[0, A^dagger],[A, 0]]. Define |z_i^pm> = (1/sqrt(2))(|0>|v_i> pm |1>|w_i>). Prove that A~ is Hermitian, that A~ |z_i^pm> = pm sigma_i |z_i^pm> (so the |z_i^pm> are a complete set of eigenvectors with eigenvalues pm sigma_i), and deduce that for an even function f, f(A~)|0>|psi> = |0> f^triangleright(A)|psi> while for an odd function f, f(A~)|0>|psi> = |1> f^diamond(A)|psi>. Explain how this shows that applying an eigenvalue transformation to the dilated matrix automatically realizes the singular value transformation of A, and why measuring the ancilla gives a definite outcome (0 for even f, 1 for odd f).
reference_answer: Hermiticity: A~^dagger = [[0, A^dagger],[A, 0]]^dagger = [[0, A^dagger],[A, 0]] = A~, since the (2,1) block A becomes (A^dagger)^dagger = A in position (1,2)... more precisely the adjoint swaps off-diagonal blocks and conjugate-transposes them: the (1,2) block A^dagger has adjoint A placed in (2,1), and the (2,1) block A has adjoint A^dagger placed in (1,2); these reproduce A~. So A~ is Hermitian. Eigenvectors: compute A~|z_i^pm> = (1/sqrt(2)) A~(|0>|v_i> pm |1>|w_i>). Using the block action A~(|0>|x>) = |1>(A|x>) and A~(|1>|y>) = |0>(A^dagger|y>) (the off-diagonal blocks move the ancilla and apply A or A^dagger): A~|0>|v_i> = |1>(A|v_i>) = sigma_i |1>|w_i>, and A~|1>|w_i> = |0>(A^dagger|w_i>) = sigma_i |0>|v_i>. Hence A~|z_i^pm> = (1/sqrt(2))(sigma_i|1>|w_i> pm sigma_i|0>|v_i>) = (sigma_i/sqrt(2))(pm|0>|v_i> + |1>|w_i>) = pm sigma_i * (1/sqrt(2))(|0>|v_i> pm |1>|w_i>) = pm sigma_i |z_i^pm>. So the |z_i^pm> are eigenvectors with eigenvalues pm sigma_i; as {|v_i>}, {|w_i>} are orthonormal bases, the {|z_i^pm>} form a complete orthonormal eigenbasis of the 2N-dimensional space. Matrix function: f(A~) = sum_i (|z_i^+> f(sigma_i) <z_i^+| + |z_i^-> f(-sigma_i) <z_i^-|). Expanding into the |0>,|1> blocks and using f_even(x) = (f(x)+f(-x))/2, f_odd(x) = (f(x)-f(-x))/2 gives f(A~) = [[ sum_i |v_i> f_even(sigma_i) <v_i|, sum_i |v_i> f_odd(sigma_i) <w_i| ],[ sum_i |w_i> f_odd(sigma_i) <v_i|, sum_i |w_i> f_even(sigma_i) <w_i| ]] = [[ f^triangleright_even(A), f^diamond_odd(A^dagger) ],[ f^diamond_odd(A), f^triangleleft_even(A) ]]. Now act on |0>|psi>: the |0> (ancilla) input picks out the first block-column. If f is EVEN, f_odd = 0, so f(A~)|0>|psi> = |0>(sum_i |v_i> f(sigma_i) <v_i|)|psi> = |0> f^triangleright(A)|psi>; the ancilla stays |0>. If f is ODD, f_even = 0, so f(A~)|0>|psi> = |1>(sum_i |w_i> f(sigma_i) <v_i|)|psi> = |1> f^diamond(A)|psi>; the ancilla flips to |1>. Interpretation: performing an eigenvalue transformation f on the Hermitian dilation A~ (which is what qubitization/QSVT does for Hermitian matrices) automatically produces, in the system register, the singular value transformation of A -- the diamond (odd) or triangleright (even) version -- because the eigenvalues of A~ are exactly the signed singular values pm sigma_i. The ancilla outcome is DEFINITE (0 for even, 1 for odd) because a definite-parity f kills one of the two parity components (f_odd or f_even), leaving the output entirely in a single ancilla branch; one therefore reads the ancilla deterministically and keeps the transformed system state with no postselection loss.

question: Not every eigenvalue transformation can be realized as a singular value transformation. Consider the matrix power f(x) = x^2 applied to a general diagonalizable but non-Hermitian matrix A = V D V^{-1} with SVD A = W Sigma V^dagger. Show by a concrete structural argument that A^2 generally CANNOT be written as a singular value transformation of A (i.e. as W g(Sigma) V^dagger, V g(Sigma) V^dagger, or W g(Sigma) W^dagger for any scalar g), by exhibiting the obstruction A^2 = W Sigma (V^dagger W) Sigma V^dagger in which the unitary factor V^dagger W does not simplify. Contrast this with the matrix inverse f(x) = x^{-1}, which IS a singular value transformation (A^{-1} = V Sigma^{-1} W^dagger = f_SV(A^dagger) with the odd f(x) = x^{-1}), and explain what property of the inverse makes it exceptional.
reference_answer: Write the SVD A = W Sigma V^dagger. Then A^2 = (W Sigma V^dagger)(W Sigma V^dagger) = W Sigma (V^dagger W) Sigma V^dagger. A singular value transformation produces one of W g(Sigma) V^dagger (balanced/diamond), V g(Sigma) V^dagger (right), or W g(Sigma) W^dagger (left): in each case the two outer unitary factors are W,V (or V,V or W,W) and the MIDDLE is a single diagonal function g(Sigma) of the singular values, with NO interior unitary between two Sigma factors. In A^2 = W Sigma (V^dagger W) Sigma V^dagger there is an interior unitary M := V^dagger W sandwiched between the two Sigma's. For a general non-Hermitian A, V and W are different unitaries and M = V^dagger W is a generic unitary that does not commute with Sigma and is not diagonal; hence Sigma M Sigma is not a function of Sigma alone -- it mixes the singular directions. There is no scalar g with Sigma M Sigma = g(Sigma) unless M is diagonal in the singular basis (which happens only in special cases, e.g. A normal so that V = W up to phases). Therefore A^2 cannot in general be put in any of the three SVT forms: the obstruction is precisely the non-trivial interior factor V^dagger W. (Concretely, for A = W Sigma V^dagger with Sigma = diag(2,1) and V^dagger W a 45-degree rotation, Sigma(V^dagger W)Sigma has off-diagonal entries, so it is not any diagonal g(Sigma).) Contrast -- the inverse is exceptional: A^{-1} = (W Sigma V^dagger)^{-1} = (V^dagger)^{-1} Sigma^{-1} W^{-1} = V Sigma^{-1} W^dagger (using V,W unitary). This has the diamond/SVT form with the outer unitaries V and W^dagger and middle diagonal Sigma^{-1} = g(Sigma) for g(x) = x^{-1}, and NO interior unitary. Equivalently, since f(x) = x^{-1} is ODD, f_SV(A^dagger) = f^diamond(A^dagger) = V Sigma^{-1} W^dagger = A^{-1}. What makes the inverse exceptional is that x^{-1} is a function applied to EACH singular value independently and the inversion of a product of unitaries-times-diagonal reverses the order WITHOUT inserting any interior unitary between two diagonals -- there is only ONE Sigma factor to transform, so no V^dagger W cross term ever appears. Powers A^k for k >= 2 (and matrix exp, log, etc.) involve PRODUCTS of A, each contributing its own W,Sigma,V^dagger, which forces interior V^dagger W factors; the inverse (a single reciprocal) is the one monomial that avoids this.

question: Let U_A in HBE_{1,m}(A) be a Hermitian block encoding of a Hermitian A with ||A|| <= 1, spectral decomposition A = sum_i lambda_i |v_i><v_i|, so that U_A |0^m>|v_i> = lambda_i |0^m>|v_i> + sqrt(1-lambda_i^2)|perp_i> with Pi|perp_i> = 0, Pi = |0^m><0^m| tensor I. For -1 < lambda_i < 1, prove that H_i = span{|0^m>|v_i>, |perp_i>} is a 2D invariant subspace of U_A on which U_A is a reflection [[lambda_i, sqrt(1-lambda_i^2)],[sqrt(1-lambda_i^2), -lambda_i]], that the iterate O = U_A Z_Pi (with Z_Pi = 2 Pi - I) acts on H_i as the rotation [[lambda_i, -sqrt(1-lambda_i^2)],[sqrt(1-lambda_i^2), lambda_i]], and hence that O^k restricted to H_i has top-left entry T_k(lambda_i) (Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind), so O^k = (U_A Z_Pi)^k is a (1,m,0)-block-encoding of T_k(A). State where Hermiticity of U_A is used.
reference_answer: Invariant subspace and reflection form: by the HBE relation, U_A|0^m>|v_i> = lambda_i|0^m>|v_i> + sqrt(1-lambda_i^2)|perp_i>, with |perp_i> normalized and orthogonal to the Pi-subspace. Since U_A is Hermitian (U_A = U_A^dagger) and U_A is unitary, U_A^2 = I. Apply U_A again to the identity above: U_A(U_A|0^m>|v_i>) = |0^m>|v_i>, i.e. lambda_i U_A|0^m>|v_i> + sqrt(1-lambda_i^2) U_A|perp_i> = |0^m>|v_i>. Substituting U_A|0^m>|v_i> and solving gives U_A|perp_i> = sqrt(1-lambda_i^2)|0^m>|v_i> - lambda_i|perp_i>. Thus both U_A|0^m>|v_i> and U_A|perp_i> lie in H_i = span{|0^m>|v_i>, |perp_i>}, so H_i is invariant, and in the ordered basis B_i = {|0^m>|v_i>, |perp_i>} the matrix of U_A is [[lambda_i, sqrt(1-lambda_i^2)],[sqrt(1-lambda_i^2), -lambda_i]], a (symmetric, trace-0, determinant -1) reflection. Hermiticity is used precisely here: applying U_A = U_A^dagger a SECOND time (via U_A^2 = I) is what produces the closed expression for U_A|perp_i> and hence the 2D invariance; without Hermiticity U_A|perp_i> need not stay in H_i. Iterate as rotation: H_i is invariant for Pi too, with [Pi]_{B_i} = [[1,0],[0,0]] (since |0^m>|v_i> is in range(Pi) and |perp_i> is orthogonal to it). Hence Z_Pi = 2Pi - I has [Z_Pi]_{B_i} = [[1,0],[0,-1]], a reflection. The iterate O = U_A Z_Pi has matrix [[lambda_i, sqrt(1-lambda_i^2)],[sqrt(1-lambda_i^2), -lambda_i]] [[1,0],[0,-1]] = [[lambda_i, -sqrt(1-lambda_i^2)],[sqrt(1-lambda_i^2), lambda_i]], which with lambda_i = cos theta_i is exactly the rotation [[cos theta_i, -sin theta_i],[sin theta_i, cos theta_i]] (product of two reflections = rotation). Chebyshev powers: therefore [O^k]_{B_i} = [[cos k theta_i, -sin k theta_i],[sin k theta_i, cos k theta_i]] = [[T_k(lambda_i), -sqrt(1-lambda_i^2) U_{k-1}(lambda_i)],[sqrt(1-lambda_i^2) U_{k-1}(lambda_i), T_k(lambda_i)]], using T_k(cos theta) = cos(k theta) and U_{k-1}(cos theta) = sin(k theta)/sin theta. The top-left entry is T_k(lambda_i). Block encoding of T_k(A): the vectors {|0^m>|v_i>} span range(Pi), and on each H_i the (0^m,0^m) component of O^k equals T_k(lambda_i). Summing over i, Pi O^k Pi = sum_i T_k(lambda_i) |0^m>|v_i><v_i|<0^m| = |0^m><0^m| tensor T_k(A). Hence (<0^m| tensor I) O^k (|0^m> tensor I) = T_k(A), i.e. O^k = (U_A Z_Pi)^k in BE_{1,m,0}(T_k(A)). (For lambda_i = pm 1 the subspace is already 1D-invariant and T_k(pm1) = (pm1)^k is reproduced trivially.)

question: Work in an exact-real word-operation model that keeps eight separate running counters: field operations, square roots, inverse-cosine calls, other trigonometric calls, exact comparisons, stored-word reads, stored-word writes, and emitted records. Each primitive call adds one unit to its own counter; proof checking, counter bookkeeping and loop-index arithmetic are free, and stored data are nested vectors. A plane rotation acts on two stored length-M real rows u and v with coefficients c and s, returning rows whose j-th entries are c*u_j - s*v_j and s*u_j + c*v_j. The implementation first materializes a stored vector of M computed entry-pairs, then materializes the first output row and the second output row as two further stored passes. Every materialized pass over M indices additionally charges two reads and two writes per index to write each intermediate value and read it back for projection, and each single entry-pair is computed with exactly the six field operations c*u_j, s*v_j, s*u_j, c*v_j, their difference, and their sum. Prove that rotating the two rows costs exactly 6*M field operations, 10*M reads and 6*M writes, and account for the origin of every read and write.
reference_answer: Count the three materialized passes separately. Pass 1 computes the entry-pairs: for each index j it reads u_j and v_j (2 reads) and performs the six field operations, so its own work is 6 field + 2 reads per index; the materialization surcharge adds 2 reads + 2 writes per index, giving 6*M field + 4*M reads + 2*M writes. Pass 2 materializes the first output row by reading the stored pair at each index (1 read) and projecting its first component (free), with surcharge 2 reads + 2 writes, giving 3*M reads + 2*M writes. Pass 3 does the same for the second component, another 3*M reads + 2*M writes. Summing: field = 6*M; reads = 4*M + 3*M + 3*M = 10*M; writes = 2*M + 2*M + 2*M = 6*M. The field count is purely the arithmetic of the rotation; the reads split into 2*M genuine input reads, 2*M pair reads for the two projections, and 6*M materialization read-backs; the writes are the three stored passes at 2*M each. This is an exact operation count in the extended exact-real model, not a finite-bit running-time bound, and it does not assert that any of these operations is physically free.

reference_answer: Add the charged subparts. Reading rows i and j from the stored matrix contributes 2 reads. Producing the two rotated rows contributes 6*M field, 10*M reads and 6*M writes. Each persistent row-replacement copies the whole length-N spine of rows, charging N reads and N writes; two replacements add 2*N reads and 2*N writes. Totals: field = 6*M; reads = 10*M + 2 + 2*N; writes = 6*M + 2*N. The 2*N read/write term is a deliberate feature of the cost contract: the model charges a full persistent row-replacement as N reads and N writes of the row-index spine. This is a stipulated charge, not a theorem that no sharing is possible; a functional persistent vector may in fact share the unaffected rows, but the model declines to credit any such copy-on-write or structural-sharing optimization and bills the full spine copy regardless. Charging it this way makes the bound robust: it holds for any implementation of row replacement without relying on aliasing analysis, and it is an exact-real word-operation count rather than a finite-bit machine running time. The 2*N term would only vanish under a model that explicitly credits in-place or shared updates, which this cost contract does not.

question: In the eight-counter exact-real model, a column sweep eliminates entries below a pivot by performing a chronological chain of elimination steps. Each step first computes an elimination angle and the two rotation coefficients (bounded by a fixed per-step budget B that is independent of which branch of the angle computation is taken), applies a rotation to the stored matrix, and then emits exactly one rotation record (one unit on the emitted-record counter). A sweep performing k steps is defined by recursion: zero steps emit nothing and do no work; a sweep of k+1 steps performs one elimination step and then recurses on the resulting matrix, emitting one record for the step. Prove by induction on k that (a) the total cost of a k-step sweep is at most k*(B + one emit) on every counter, and (b) the emitted-record counter equals exactly k, even though some steps may rotate by a harmless zero angle.
reference_answer: Argue by induction on the number of steps k. Base case k=0: the sweep returns the input unchanged with zero cost on every counter, so both the bound 0*(B+emit) and the exact emit count 0 hold. Inductive step k+1: by the recursive definition the sweep cost equals the cost of one elimination step, plus the cost of the k-step sweep on the updated matrix, plus one emitted record. For (a), the single step is bounded by B on every counter (the per-step budget already absorbs the branch-independent angle budget, both rotation coefficients, the rotation, and the stored reads), the recursive part is bounded by k*(B+emit) by the induction hypothesis, and the emit contributes one unit; adding gives at most (k+1)*(B+emit) on every counter. For (b), the single step emits exactly one record and the recursive sweep emits exactly k by hypothesis, with no other operation touching the emit counter, so the total is exactly k+1. The exact emit equality holds regardless of the actual angles because a zero-angle rotation still produces and emits its record; the step budget B is only an upper bound on the arithmetic counters, so the two claims are of different strengths: an exact count for emissions and an inequality for the rest.

question: In the eight-counter exact-real model, a bounded sum over an index set of size k is evaluated by a monadic fold: starting from the pure value zero (no charge), each of the k summands is produced and then added to the running accumulator with one field addition. Suppose every summand has the same per-counter cost B. Prove that the whole sum costs exactly k*(B + one field operation). Then specialize to a single contraction entry over a bond of size D, where each summand reads one entry of a stored core (two reads) and one entry of a stored vector (one read) and multiplies them (one field), so B is three reads plus one field, and conclude that the entry costs exactly D*(three reads + two field operations).
reference_answer: Induct on k. Base case k=0: the empty sum is the pure zero with no charge, matching 0*(B+field). Inductive step: a sum over k+1 indices produces the first summand (cost B), binds an addition of it to the recursively evaluated tail (that addition is one field operation), and the tail is a sum over k indices. By the induction hypothesis the tail costs k*(B+field); adding the first summand's B and the one field for its combination gives B + field + k*(B+field) = (k+1)*(B+field). So the sum costs exactly k*(B+field) on every counter. For the contraction entry: each summand reads a stored core entry, which is a row read followed by an entry read (two reads), reads one stored vector entry (one read), and multiplies the two values (one field), so B = three reads + one field. Substituting into the law gives D*((three reads + one field) + one field) = D*(three reads + two field operations). The second field per index is exactly the accumulation addition, which is why the entry has two field operations per bond index rather than one. This is an exact count in the extended exact-real model, not a finite-bit cost.

question: A stored matrix-product chain over n+1 cores, each of bond size D, is closed into a scalar-boundary chain in two conceptual halves. First the tail is processed recursively: at the last position the terminal core is contracted against a right boundary vector, and at every earlier position the current core is kept while the remaining table is copied by reference and the tail is recursed; a fixed small per-node record is charged at each position. Second the leftmost core is contracted against a left boundary vector. The returned chain exactly refines the kernel chain contracted against the two boundary vectors. Prove that the summed cost of the whole closure is bounded by a polynomial that is quadratic in the chain length n and cubic-free but quadratic in the bond D, and explain why the tail recursion contributes an n-squared term while the single left closure contributes only a bond-dependent term with no dependence on n.

The terminal contraction at the last position contracts a D-by-D core against a length-D vector, costing on the order of D-squared field and read work plus boundary materialization, a fixed function of D. Each earlier position copies the remaining table of references (cost linear in the number of remaining cores, i.e. linear in the position index) and charges a fixed node record; summing the reference-copy cost over the n earlier positions gives an arithmetic series that is quadratic in n, which is the source of the n-squared term, while the fixed node records contribute a term linear in n. Hence the tail total is bounded by a constant times D-squared plus a constant plus terms 5*n-squared + 7*n + constant. The left closure performs exactly one initial contraction of a D-by-D core against a length-D left vector plus one node record; this is a single bond-dependent cost with no sum over positions, hence no n dependence. Adding the two halves gives the closure bound 20*D-squared + 30*D + 5*n-squared + 7*n + constant. The decoupling is structural: the tail walks the whole chain so its copying accumulates with length, whereas the left boundary touches only the one leftmost core. All of this is counted in the extended exact-real word model, not as finite-bit running time, and the referenced cores are already materialized so no kernel callback is evaluated.

native_nl.core_summary: Prove the sum-over-tags total equals the eight-term enumerated total, is additive, zero on the zero cost and one on a unit charge, and explain why this enables compositional cost proofs.

question: Two notions of total cost appear in the stored exact-real model. One, call it the ordinary total, is the sum of a cost function over the finite type of all operation tags. The other, call it the enumerated total, is the explicit eight-term sum field + square root + inverse-cosine + other-trig + comparison + read + write + emitted-record. Prove that these two totals are equal as functions of the cost, that the total of a sum of two costs is the sum of their totals, that the total of the zero cost is zero, and that the total of a single unit charge on one tag is one. Explain why these simple algebraic facts are exactly what licenses replacing a sum-over-tags by the fixed eight-term expression in later cost proofs.
reference_answer: The operation tags form a finite type with exactly the eight inhabitants field, square root, inverse-cosine, other-trig, comparison, read, write, emitted-record. The ordinary total sums the cost over the universal finite set of tags. Enumerating that finite set as the eight listed inhabitants, the sum over the set equals field + sqrt + angle + trig + compare + read + write + emit, which is precisely the enumerated total; hence the two totals coincide for every cost. Additivity: the sum over tags of (a+b) applied pointwise is the sum over tags of a plus the sum over tags of b, because finite summation distributes over pointwise addition; so the total of a sum is the sum of the totals. Zero: the zero cost assigns zero to every tag, and a finite sum of zeros is zero. Unit charge: a single unit charge on one tag assigns one to that tag and zero to the others, so its total over all tags is exactly one. question: A primitive quantum circuit is a chronological list of gates, each gate acting on a set of touched wires. A per-wire scheduling fold tracks, for every wire, the earliest layer at which its next gate can be placed: processing a gate pushes every touched wire to one more than the maximum current depth over the gate's touched wires, and leaves untouched wires unchanged. The circuit depth is the maximum over all wires of the final per-wire depths; the gate count is the length of the list. Identify the key per-step inequality that drives the induction.
reference_answer: The key per-step fact is: if every wire currently has depth at most some bound, then after processing one gate every wire has depth at most that bound plus one. For a touched wire the new depth is one plus the maximum current depth over the touched wires; since each of those is at most the bound, their maximum is at most the bound, so the new depth is at most bound plus one. For an untouched wire the depth is unchanged, hence at most the bound and so at most bound plus one. Now induct on the gate list to bound the folded profile: starting from the all-zero profile (every wire at most 0), each of the L gates raises the uniform upper bound by at most one, so after the whole circuit every wire has depth at most 0 + L = L, the gate count. Taking the maximum over wires, the circuit depth is at most L. Finally the reported resource depth is defined to equal this scheduling depth, so it too is at most the gate count. This bounds a genuine parallel-scheduling depth, computed by the per-wire fold rather than assigned as a serial surrogate; equality can fail because parallelizable gates on disjoint wires share a layer, making the true depth strictly smaller than the gate count.

question: A stored N-by-M matrix is built by materializing an entry supplier: for each of the N*M entries the supplier is run to produce a value, and the construction charges, on top of the supplier's own counted work, two reads and two writes per entry plus two reads and two writes per row to store and project. reference_answer: The claim is false because the cost identity contains the double sum of the supplier's own per-entry costs, which is not determined by N and M alone. Counterexample: let the supplier for entry (i,j) perform j additional field operations (say by summing j stored values before returning). Then the supplier's per-entry cost is not constant, and the double sum of field operations equals the sum over i of (0+1+...+(M-1)) = N*M*(M-1)/2 field operations, which depends on the internal structure of the supplier, not merely on the surcharge. Two different suppliers producing matrices of the same dimensions can therefore have different total costs, so no fixed polynomial in N and M alone bounds every materialization. Indeed the source flags the input callback as an explicit boundary: the constructor charges storage but does not certify the callback's scalar evaluation cost. The correct statement is conditional: if the supplier's per-entry cost is bounded by a uniform value B on every counter, then the materialization is bounded by N*M*B plus (N*M + N) times the surcharge; only after supplying such a per-entry bound B does a polynomial-in-dimensions bound follow. All of this is in the exact-real operation model and makes no finite-bit claim; the moral is that materialization cost cleanly separates the surcharge (fixed by dimensions) from the supplier work (which must be separately bounded).

question: A stored matrix-product chain is assembled from n+1 stored cores, each of bond size D, closed against left and right boundary vectors of length D to form a scalar-boundary chain. It is proved that the maximum bond of the resulting chain is at most the maximum of D and one. Interpret this bond bound as a statement about the represented object, explain why the maximum with one appears, and determine the boundary values of D for which the bond equals one rather than D. Also state what this does and does not say about the cost of building the chain.
reference_answer: The bond bound says the assembled chain never develops an internal bond larger than the input core bond D, except that the two scalar boundaries contribute trivial bonds of size one. Concretely the closure contracts the end cores against length-D vectors, collapsing the two outer bonds to one while leaving the interior bonds at most D; taking the maximum over all bonds gives at most the maximum of D and one. The maximum with one appears precisely because of the degenerate boundary: a scalar-boundary chain has outer bonds of dimension one, so even if an interior bond were zero or the chain degenerate, the reported maximum bond cannot drop below one. The boundary analysis: for D at least one the maximum of D and one is just D, so the bond bound is simply D; the maximum with one only becomes active, giving bond one, in the degenerate case D equal to zero, where there are no interior bonds and only the unit scalar boundaries remain. Regarding cost, this is a statement about the stored object's structure (its bonds), not its construction cost: it certifies that contraction does not inflate the bond dimension, but it says nothing by itself about the number of exact-real operations spent building the chain, which is bounded separately; and it is not a finite-bit claim.

native_nl.core_summary: A single Taylor-truncation polynomial reproduces every prescribed derivative up to order k exactly, via the j! normalization of Taylor coefficients.

question: Fix a real point a and a natural number k, and prescribe target values v(0), v(1), ..., v(k). Define a degree-at-most-k real polynomial P by taking the local Taylor polynomial centred at a whose coefficient of (x-a)^j is v(j)/j!. Prove that for every j with 0 <= j <= k the ordinary j-th derivative of P evaluated at a equals exactly v(j). You may use the fact that the j-th derivative of a polynomial at a point equals j! times the degree-j Taylor coefficient of the polynomial about that point.
reference_answer: Write P = sum over i in {0,...,k} of (v(i)/i!) * (x-a)^i. The key bridge is that for any polynomial Q, (d^j/dx^j Q)(a) = j! * c_j, where c_j is the coefficient of (x-a)^j in the Taylor expansion of Q about a; equivalently c_j is the degree-j coefficient of the shifted polynomial Q(x+a). Step 1: the Taylor coefficients of P about a are read off directly: the coefficient of (x-a)^j is v(j)/j! for j <= k and 0 for j > k, because P is already written in the (x-a) basis. Step 2: apply the bridge at order j <= k: (d^j P/dx^j)(a) = j! * (coefficient of (x-a)^j) = j! * (v(j)/j!). Step 3: since j! is a nonzero natural number cast into the reals, j! * (v(j)/j!) = v(j) exactly. Hence every requested jet value is reproduced, and the construction has degree at most k, has degree at most k. The bound k is the generic (worst-case) degree needed to carry k+1 derivative constraints at a single node; particular data may be realised by a lower-degree polynomial (all-zero data gives the zero polynomial, and if v(k)=0 the degree drops below k), so k is an upper bound on this construction's degree, not a universal minimum for every data vector. No approximation is involved: the identities are exact real-polynomial identities.

question: Let p and q be real polynomials and a a real point. Suppose (x-a)^{k+1} divides the difference p-q. Prove that for every order j with 0 <= j <= k, the j-th derivatives of p and q agree at a: (d^j p/dx^j)(a) = (d^j q/dx^j)(a). Explain precisely why the hypothesis forces agreement of all jets strictly below the multiplicity k+1, and why it says nothing about the j = k+1 derivative in general.
reference_answer: Set r = p - q, so (x-a)^{k+1} | r. Step 1 (differentiation lowers the zero order by at most j): differentiating a function with a zero of order m at a exactly j times leaves a zero of order at least m-j; formally, (x-a)^{m-j} divides the j-th derivative of r whenever (x-a)^m | r. With m = k+1 and j <= k we get m-j = k+1-j >= 1. Step 2: therefore (x-a)^{k+1-j} divides (d^j r/dx^j); since k+1-j >= 1, in particular (x-a)^1 = (x-a) divides the j-th derivative of r. Step 3: a polynomial divisible by (x-a) vanishes at a; evaluating (d^j r/dx^j) at a gives 0. Step 4: derivatives are linear, so (d^j r/dx^j)(a) = (d^j p/dx^j)(a) - (d^j q/dx^j)(a) = 0, i.e. the jets agree. Why only below the multiplicity: at j = k+1 we have m-j = 0, so the argument only yields (x-a)^0 = 1 dividing the derivative, a vacuous statement; the (k+1)-th derivatives need not agree. Concretely p - q = (x-a)^{k+1} has k-th derivative 0 at a but nonzero (k+1)-th derivative (k+1)!, witnessing that the bound is sharp.

question: Consider the generating power series obtained as the product of the exponential series exp(X) and the series 1/(1-X)^{k+1}. Let its degree-r coefficient be a_{k,r}. In the coordinate t, define A_k(t) as the truncation of this series to degrees 0..k, i.e. A_k(t) = sum_{r=0}^{k} a_{k,r} t^r. The source polynomial, in the shifted coordinate t = p+1, is a positive combination S(p) = exp(-1) * (1-t)^{k+1} * A_k(t) + t^{k+1} * A_k(1-t). Prove that A_k(t) > 0 for every t >= 0, and deduce that S(p) > 0 for every p in the closed interval [-1, 0].
reference_answer: Step 1 (coefficients are nonnegative): the coefficient a_{k,r} equals the Cauchy product sum_{m=0}^{r} (1/m!) * C(k+r-m, k), where C denotes a binomial coefficient coming from 1/(1-X)^{k+1} = sum C(k+i, k) X^i and 1/m! from exp. Each summand is a quotient of nonnegative reals, so a_{k,r} >= 0, and a_{k,0} = C(k,k)/0! = 1 > 0. Step 2 (positivity of A_k on t >= 0): A_k(t) = sum_{r=0}^{k} a_{k,r} t^r is a finite sum of nonnegative terms a_{k,r} t^r (products of nonnegative a_{k,r} and nonnegative t^r). The r=0 term is a_{k,0} = 1, which is strictly positive, so the whole sum is at least 1 > 0. Step 3 (positivity of S on [-1,0]): put t = p+1. For p in [-1,0] we have t in [0,1], so both t >= 0 and 1-t >= 0. Then A_k(t) > 0 and A_k(1-t) > 0 by Step 2. The prefactors exp(-1) > 0, (1-t)^{k+1} >= 0, t^{k+1} >= 0 are nonnegative. Step 4 (strictness): if t = 0 the second term vanishes but the first is exp(-1) * 1 * A_k(0) > 0; otherwise t > 0 makes t^{k+1} * A_k(1-t) > 0, so one term is always strictly positive while the other is nonnegative. Hence S(p) > 0 throughout [-1,0].

question: Two real polynomials p and q both have degree at most 2k+1, and both satisfy the same two-point jet data: all derivatives through order k agree at the node -1, and all derivatives through order k agree at the node 0. Prove that p = q. Structure the argument around the two 'endpoint multiplicity' polynomials (x+1)^{k+1} and x^{k+1}, and explain where coprimality and the degree budget 2k+1 enter.
reference_answer: Step 1 (each endpoint gives a divisibility): since p and q share all jets through order k at -1, the difference p-q has a zero of order at least k+1 at -1, i.e. (x+1)^{k+1} divides p-q. The equivalence used is: agreement of all derivatives through order k at a point a is equivalent to (x-a)^{k+1} dividing the difference (one direction is the high-multiplicity-zero fact; the converse is proved by reading Taylor coefficients, all of which through degree k vanish). The same at 0 gives x^{k+1} divides p-q. Step 2 (coprimality combines the two): (x+1)^{k+1} and x^{k+1} are coprime because their bases x+1 and x differ by a unit (their difference is 1), and coprimality is preserved under taking powers. For coprime factors each dividing the same element, their product divides it; hence (x+1)^{k+1} * x^{k+1} divides p-q. Step 3 (degree accounting forces zero difference): the product has degree (k+1)+(k+1) = 2k+2. If p-q were nonzero, a nonzero multiple of a degree-(2k+2) polynomial would have degree at least 2k+2. But deg(p-q) <= max(deg p, deg q) <= 2k+1 < 2k+2, a contradiction. Therefore p-q = 0, i.e. p = q. The degree budget 2k+1 is exactly one below the combined multiplicity 2k+2, which is what makes the only common solution the zero difference; coprimality is what lets the two separate divisibilities multiply.

question: A colleague claims that the two-point jet data 'all derivatives through order k agree at -1 and at 0' pins down a real polynomial uniquely, with no restriction on its degree. Show this is false by exhibiting an explicit nonzero polynomial of degree 2k+2 all of whose derivatives through order k vanish at both -1 and 0. Conclude that the degree bound 2k+1 in the uniqueness statement cannot be dropped, and state the exact dimension of the space of polynomials sharing a fixed set of such endpoint jets.
reference_answer: Counterexample: take E(x) = (x+1)^{k+1} * x^{k+1}, a polynomial of degree (k+1)+(k+1) = 2k+2. Step 1: at the node -1, E has the factor (x+1)^{k+1}, i.e. a zero of order k+1 there; hence all derivatives of E through order k vanish at -1 (a zero of order k+1 kills derivatives 0..k). Symmetrically the factor x^{k+1} makes all derivatives through order k vanish at 0. So E carries the all-zero endpoint jet data, exactly the data that the zero polynomial also carries. Step 2: E is not the zero polynomial (it is monic of degree 2k+2), so if p is any solution of a given jet-data problem, p + E is a different polynomial with identical endpoint jets. Thus the solution is not unique once degree 2k+2 is allowed; the colleague's claim fails. Step 3 (exact structure): the solutions of fixed endpoint jet data form a coset of the ideal generated by E = (x+1)^{k+1} x^{k+1}. Within any degree bound 2k+1 the coset meets the degree-<=2k+1 space in exactly one point (that is the uniqueness theorem). Allowing degree 2k+2 adds the one-dimensional direction spanned by E, and more generally allowing degree 2k+1+d adds a d-dimensional family (multiples of E by polynomials of degree < d). So the degree-2k+1 budget is sharp: it is the largest budget on which the jet data has a unique solution.

question: Let the generating series be C(X) = exp(X) * (1 - X)^{-(k+1)} as formal power series over the reals. Prove that its coefficient of X^r is exactly sum_{m=0}^{r} C(k + r - m, k) / m!, where C(.,.) is the binomial coefficient, and prove that this coefficient is nonnegative for every r, with the r=0 coefficient equal to 1. You may use that exp(X) has coefficient 1/m! in degree m and that (1-X)^{-(k+1)} has coefficient C(k+i, k) in degree i.
reference_answer: Step 1 (Cauchy product): the coefficient of X^r in a product of two power series F*G is the convolution sum_{m=0}^{r} [X^m]F * [X^{r-m}]G. Here [X^m] exp = 1/m! and [X^{i}] (1-X)^{-(k+1)} = C(k+i, k). Step 2 (substitute i = r-m): the convolution becomes sum_{m=0}^{r} (1/m!) * C(k + (r-m), k) = sum_{m=0}^{r} C(k+r-m, k)/m!, which is the asserted closed form. The index substitution is valid because as m ranges over 0..r the complementary index r-m ranges over r..0, covering the same antidiagonal. Step 3 (nonnegativity): every summand is a ratio of a nonnegative binomial coefficient and a positive factorial, hence nonnegative; a finite sum of nonnegative reals is nonnegative. Step 4 (value at r=0): the sum collapses to the single term m=0, giving C(k, k)/0! = 1/1 = 1. This closed form is what makes the truncation A_k the exact finite object underlying the positive source polynomial, and its nonnegativity is exactly the ingredient needed downstream for positivity.

question: In the shifted coordinate t = p + 1, the source Hermite bridge polynomial is written as a sum of two endpoint contributions: S(p) = exp(-1) * (1-t)^{k+1} * A_k(t) + t^{k+1} * A_k(1-t), where A_k is a fixed degree-<=k polynomial. Explain the structural role of each ingredient: why the coordinate is centred so that the two nodes p = -1 and p = 0 become t = 0 and t = 1, why each term carries a factor raised to the power k+1, how the two terms specialise the required endpoint values exp(-1) at p=-1 and 1 at p=0, and why the construction is manifestly symmetric under the reflection t -> 1-t up to the constant exp(-1).
reference_answer: The coordinate t = p+1 maps the physical splice interval p in [-1,0] onto t in [0,1], sending the left node p=-1 to t=0 and the right node p=0 to t=1; this normalises the two interpolation nodes to the unit interval endpoints. Each term is a product of a 'vanishing' factor and a 'value-carrying' factor. In the first term, (1-t)^{k+1} vanishes to order k+1 at t=1 (the right node), so the entire first term and all its derivatives through order k vanish at p=0; thus the first term is responsible only for the left node. At t=0 the first term equals exp(-1) * 1 * A_k(0); because A_k(0) is the degree-0 coefficient of the generating series, which is 1, the first term contributes exactly exp(-1) at the left node, matching the required left endpoint value exp(-1). Symmetrically the second term t^{k+1} vanishes to order k+1 at t=0 (left node), so it only affects the right node, where it equals 1^{k+1} * A_k(0) = 1, matching the required right endpoint value 1 (= (-1)^0). The power k+1 is what guarantees each term's derivatives through order k vanish at the opposite node, decoupling the two endpoints' jet data. Finally the construction is symmetric under t -> 1-t: this reflection swaps the two terms (and swaps A_k(t) with A_k(1-t), and (1-t)^{k+1} with t^{k+1}), the only asymmetry being the scalar exp(-1) weighting the left value versus 1 on the right. This mirrors the physical left/right exponential tails exp(p) and exp(-p) meeting the polynomial bridge.

The denominator C(2k+1,i+j) of w cancels the binomial in B, leaving C(k-i,j) t^{i+j} (1-t)^{2k+1-i-j}. Writing 2k+1-i-j = (k+1) + (k-i-j), this is t^i (1-t)^{k+1} * [C(k-i,j) t^j (1-t)^{(k-i)-j}]. Step 2 (sum over j via binomial theorem): summing over j=0..k-i, the bracketed terms are exactly the binomial expansion of (t + (1-t))^{k-i} weighted by C(k-i,j): sum_j C(k-i,j) t^j (1-t)^{(k-i)-j} = (t+(1-t))^{k-i} = 1. Hence the sum equals t^i (1-t)^{k+1} * 1, proving the elevation identity. Step 3 (nonnegativity of coefficients): the source polynomial's left endpoint factor is sum_i a_{k,i} t^i (1-t)^{k+1} with a_{k,i} >= 0 (the generating-series coefficients). Collecting the degree-elevated contributions assigns to each Bernstein index r a coefficient that is a sum of products a_{k,i} * w(k,i,j) with i+j=r; each factor is nonnegative (a_{k,i} >= 0 and w = C(k-i,j)/C(2k+1,i+j) >= 0), so every Bernstein coefficient is nonnegative. The full source polynomial adds a reflected copy (weight exp(-1) > 0) with the same nonnegativity, so its complete Bernstein coefficient vector is nonnegative. Nonnegativity on [0,1] matters because the Bernstein basis functions are themselves nonnegative there, so a nonnegative coefficient vector certifies the polynomial is nonnegative on [0,1] without evaluating it.

native_nl.core_summary: Left de Casteljau subdivision at u reparametrises a Bernstein polynomial to u*t exactly, proved by a semiconjugacy of the linear step operator iterated d times.

question: A degree-d polynomial is held as a coefficient row c(0),...,c(d) in the Bernstein basis, so that its value at t is sum_{r=0}^{d} c(r) B_{d,r}(t). One de Casteljau step with parameter s replaces the row c by the row with entries (1-s) c(i) + s c(i+1). Let L_u denote the operation that reads the left edge of the de Casteljau triangle built with parameter u (its i-th output is the result of i de Casteljau steps at u applied to c, read at position 0). Prove that evaluating the L_u-transformed coefficients at parameter t reproduces the original polynomial at the rescaled parameter u*t: sum_r (L_u c)(r) B_{d,r}(t) = sum_r c(r) B_{d,r}(u t).
reference_answer: Model the Bernstein state as an infinite coefficient row acted on by the linear 'de Casteljau step' operator T_s := (1-s) * Id + s * Shift, where Shift sends c(i) to c(i+1). The i-th left-edge output is (T_u^i c)(0), so L_u c = (i -> (T_u^i c)(0)). Step 1 (parameter composition): a single step at a scaled parameter factors as T_{u t} = (1-t) * Id + t * T_u. This is checked entrywise: ((1-t)Id + t T_u) c (i) = (1-t) c(i) + t[(1-u)c(i) + u c(i+1)] = (1 - u t) c(i) + u t c(i+1) = T_{u t} c (i). Step 2 (semiconjugacy): consequently L_u intertwines the step at scaled parameter with the step at t: L_u (T_{u t} c) = T_t (L_u c). This is the operator identity that says applying one scaled step then taking the left edge equals taking the left edge then applying one unscaled step. Step 3 (iterate the semiconjugacy d times): because L_u is a semiconjugacy from T_{u t} to T_t, it intertwines their d-th iterates: L_u (T_{u t}^d c) = T_t^d (L_u c). Reading position 0 of both sides gives (T_t^d (L_u c))(0) = (T_{u t}^d c)(0). Step 4 (translate to Bernstein sums): the left-edge-at-0 of a d-fold de Casteljau triangle equals the Bernstein sum, i.e. (T_s^d c)(0) = sum_{r=0}^{d} c(r) B_{d,r}(s). Applying this with the row L_u c and parameter t on the left, and with c and parameter u t on the right, yields exactly sum_r (L_u c)(r) B_{d,r}(t) = sum_r c(r) B_{d,r}(u t). This is the exact affine-restriction law: left de Casteljau subdivision reparametrises the curve to [0,u].

native_nl.core_summary: De Casteljau subinterval restriction keeps every Bernstein coefficient inside the original range, because each new coefficient is a convex combination (partition of unity plus nonnegativity).

question: Let a degree-d polynomial be given by Bernstein coefficients c(0),...,c(d), all lying in a common interval [lo, hi]. Suppose we restrict the polynomial to a subinterval [u, v] with 0 <= u < v <= 1 by two successive de Casteljau subdivisions, producing new Bernstein coefficients c'(0),...,c'(d) for the restricted piece. Prove that every restricted coefficient c'(i) still lies in [lo, hi]. Identify the two structural facts about the Bernstein basis that make this true.
reference_answer: Two facts drive the proof. Fact A (partition of unity): the Bernstein basis functions of a fixed degree sum to 1 at every t, i.e. sum_{r=0}^{d} B_{d,r}(t) = 1. Fact B (nonnegativity on [0,1]): each B_{d,r}(t) >= 0 for t in [0,1]. Together they say that any Bernstein sum sum_r c(r) B_{d,r}(t) with t in [0,1] is a convex combination of the c(r), hence lies between min and max of the coefficients; in particular if all c(r) in [lo,hi] the value lies in [lo,hi]. Step 1 (one subdivision preserves bounds): each new coefficient produced by a single de Casteljau subdivision at a parameter in [0,1] is itself a Bernstein sum of a sub-row of the original coefficients evaluated at that parameter. By Facts A and B it is a convex combination of coefficients from [lo,hi], hence in [lo,hi]. This applies to the right-edge (upper) subdivision at u in [0,1]: all its outputs stay in [lo,hi]. Step 2 (second subdivision): the left-edge (lower) subdivision is applied at the parameter (v-u)/(1-u). Because 0 <= u < v <= 1 we have 0 <= (v-u)/(1-u) <= 1 (the numerator is nonnegative and at most the positive denominator 1-u). So the second subdivision is again evaluated at a parameter in [0,1], and by the same convex-combination argument its outputs — the restricted coefficients c'(i) — remain in [lo,hi]. Step 3 (conclusion): composing the two bound-preserving subdivisions keeps every c'(i) in [lo,hi]. This is the exact numerical-stability property of de Casteljau subdivision: restricting to a subinterval never amplifies coefficients beyond the original range, in contrast to monomial-basis restriction which can.

question: Let q be a real polynomial and consider sampling it on an arithmetic progression x_j = start + step * j for j = 0,1,...,count-1. We want the exact discrete squared mass M = sum_{j=0}^{count-1} q(x_j)^2 as a closed-form expression whose size depends on the degree of q, not on count. Let g(x) = q(start + step*x)^2, a polynomial of degree D = 2*deg(q), with coefficients g_0,...,g_D. Using the power-sum identity sum_{j=0}^{count-1} j^r = P_r(count) (a fixed polynomial in count, e.g. the Faulhaber/Bernoulli formula), prove the exact identity M = sum_{r=0}^{D} g_r * P_r(count), and explain why this is an exact algebraic equality rather than a quadrature approximation.
reference_answer: Step 1 (expand the square as a polynomial): g(x) = q(start + step*x)^2 is a polynomial in x; write it in the monomial basis g(x) = sum_{r=0}^{D} g_r x^r, where D = deg(g) = 2*deg(q) because squaring doubles the degree and the affine substitution x -> start + step*x does not raise degree. Then q(x_j)^2 = g(j) = sum_{r=0}^{D} g_r j^r, evaluating g at the integer index j. Step 2 (sum over samples and swap orders): M = sum_{j=0}^{count-1} g(j) = sum_{j} sum_{r=0}^{D} g_r j^r. Both sums are finite, so Fubini for finite sums lets us exchange them: M = sum_{r=0}^{D} g_r (sum_{j=0}^{count-1} j^r). Step 3 (insert the closed power sum): by the Faulhaber identity sum_{j=0}^{count-1} j^r = P_r(count), a fixed polynomial in count given by Bernoulli numbers. Substituting gives M = sum_{r=0}^{D} g_r P_r(count), a sum of only D+1 = 2 deg(q)+1 terms, independent of count. Step 4 (exactness): every step is an identity between polynomials evaluated at integers — expansion of the square, the finite exchange of summation, and the Faulhaber identity, which is itself an exact theorem (not an asymptotic or Euler-Maclaurin approximation). The only requirement is that the coefficient index runs up to a bound at least D, so that g is fully captured; the identity holds for every count including count = 0 (empty sum = 0 and P_r(0) = 0). Hence M is reproduced exactly with a degree-sized expression, with no continuum/quadrature substitution.

native_nl.core_summary: The exponential-tail discrete squared mass is a geometric sum whose closed form requires an explicit step=0 branch where the common ratio is one, with both branches agreeing in the limit.

question: On the exponential tail of the target, the sampled amplitude at x_j = start + step*j is exp(x_j), and the discrete squared mass over count samples is E = sum_{j=0}^{count-1} exp(x_j)^2. Give the exact closed form for E, and treat the boundary case step = 0 explicitly. Explain precisely why the generic geometric-series formula exp(2 start) * ((exp(2 step))^count - 1) / (exp(2 step) - 1) is well defined exactly when step is nonzero, what it degenerates to as the ratio approaches 1, and what the correct value is when step = 0.
reference_answer: Rewrite each squared term: exp(x_j)^2 = exp(2 x_j) = exp(2 start + 2 step j) = exp(2 start) * (exp(2 step))^j. So E = exp(2 start) * sum_{j=0}^{count-1} q^j with common ratio q = exp(2 step). Generic case (step != 0): since exp is injective and 2 step != 0, we have exp(2 step) != 1, so the ratio q != 1 and the finite geometric sum has the closed form sum_{j=0}^{count-1} q^j = (q^count - 1)/(q - 1). Hence E = exp(2 start) * ((exp(2 step))^count - 1)/(exp(2 step) - 1). The denominator exp(2 step) - 1 is nonzero exactly because step != 0, which is what makes the division well defined. Boundary case (step = 0): then q = exp(0) = 1 and every term equals exp(2 start), so the sum is count copies: E = count * exp(2 start). The generic formula is undefined here (its denominator is 0), so a separate branch is mandatory; this is not a removable notational nuisance but a genuine 0/0 at step = 0. The two branches agree in the limit: as step -> 0 the generic expression tends to exp(2 start) * count by L'Hopital/the limit of (q^count-1)/(q-1) at q=1, matching the step=0 value, so the piecewise definition is continuous across the boundary. A single formula without the case split would either divide by zero at step = 0 or silently return a wrong value, so the explicit boundary branch is required for a total, correct definition.

question: The target function is strictly positive everywhere and passes through the value 1 at the physical point p = 0 (the splice point). On a register of n+1 qubits the grid has 2^{n+1} points indexed in little-endian order, and the central index 2^n maps to the grid point p = 0. Prove that the unnormalized squared sample norm N = sum_j (amplitude at grid point j)^2 is at least 1, uniformly in the smoothing order k, the width n, and the physical scale L > 0. reference_answer: Step 1 (locate a unit sample): the central index c = 2^n on n+1 qubits maps, under the little-endian grid p_j = -pi L + j * (2 pi L / 2^{n+1}), to the point p = 0. Indeed j = 2^n gives -pi L + 2^n * (2 pi L / 2^{n+1}) = -pi L + pi L = 0, independent of L. Step 2 (value at the splice): the sampled amplitude at p = 0 is the target value there. On the middle branch the target equals the source polynomial, whose value at p = 0 is its order-0 right-endpoint jet, which is prescribed to be (-1)^0 = 1. Hence the central sample equals 1 exactly, for every k, n, L. Step 3 (single-term lower bound): N = sum_j a_j^2 is a sum of nonnegative squares. The term at the central index is a_c^2 = 1^2 = 1. A sum of nonnegative reals is at least any one of its terms (drop the others, which are >= 0). Therefore N >= 1. Step 4 (role of positivity): the inequality itself only needs a_c^2 = 1 and that the remaining terms are >= 0 — the latter holds for any squares. Strict positivity of all samples is a separate, stronger structural fact; here it guarantees that the full norm is genuinely bounded below by a real sample rather than by a positivity oracle, i.e. the conditioning anchor is realised by an actual grid point, and simultaneously ensures the normalizer is nonzero so normalization is well defined. The bound is width-uniform precisely because the central point stays at p = 0 for every n and L, so the unit sample never disappears as the register grows.

native_nl.core_summary: An additive polynomial array q(u(x)+v(y)) factorizes with inner dimension deg(q)+1 via shifted Taylor coefficients, bounding its rank by the degree alone.

question: Consider a bivariate real array F(x,y) = q(u(x) + v(y)), where q is a real polynomial of degree at most d and u, v are arbitrary real-valued functions of the row index x and column index y respectively. Prove that F factorizes as a matrix product A * B with inner dimension d+1, and conclude that the rank of F is at most d+1. Make explicit which polynomial identity provides the factorization and why only the degree of q — not the number of rows or columns — controls the inner dimension.
reference_answer: Step 1 (shifted-Taylor expansion of an additive argument): fix a row x and let a = u(x). Expand q about a: for any real s, q(a + s) = sum_{i=0}^{d} c_i(a) s^i, where c_i(a) is the degree-i coefficient of the Taylor expansion of q about a (the sum stops at d because deg q <= d, so the shifted polynomial also has degree <= d). Step 2 (separate the variables): apply this with a = u(x) and s = v(y): F(x,y) = q(u(x) + v(y)) = sum_{i=0}^{d} c_i(u(x)) * v(y)^i. Each summand is a product of a function of x alone, A(x,i) := c_i(u(x)), and a function of y alone, B(i,y) := v(y)^i. Step 3 (read off the matrix product): define A as the (number of rows) by (d+1) matrix with entries A(x,i) and B as the (d+1) by (number of columns) matrix with entries B(i,y). Then (A B)(x,y) = sum_{i=0}^{d} A(x,i) B(i,y) = F(x,y), i.e. F = A * B exactly, with inner dimension d+1. Step 4 (rank bound): the rank of a product A*B is at most the number of columns of A, which is d+1; equivalently the inner dimension bounds the rank. Hence rank F <= d+1. Why the inner dimension is degree-controlled: the only data that produce the finite factorization are the d+1 Taylor coefficients of q; the number of distinct values of u and v (i.e. the matrix dimensions) is irrelevant. The additive structure u(x)+v(y) is essential — it is what lets the single-variable Taylor expansion separate the two indices into a sum of d+1 rank-one pieces. A generic bivariate function without this additive polynomial structure would have no such bound.

native_nl.core_summary: Finite-width factorizations form an algebra: sum adds widths, Hadamard product multiplies them, negation and scaling preserve them, letting composite width bounds be assembled symbolically.

question: A bivariate array is said to 'factor through width w' if it can be written as a product of a (rows x w) and a (w x cols) matrix. Explain how four composition laws combine finite-width factorizations, and give the exact width each produces: (i) a sum of two arrays factoring through widths w1 and w2; (ii) the negation of an array factoring through w; (iii) the entrywise (Hadamard) product of arrays factoring through w1 and w2; (iv) a constant scalar multiple of an array factoring through w. Then explain how these laws let one assemble a width bound for a function built as a sum of products of a threshold indicator, an exponential, and a polynomial, without ever forming a dense matrix.
reference_answer: The four laws: (i) Sum: if F factors through width w1 and G through w2, then F + G factors through width w1 + w2. One stacks the left factors side by side and the right factors on top of each other (direct sum of inner index sets), so the new inner dimension adds. (ii) Negation: if F factors through w, then -F factors through the same width w; negate one factor (e.g. the left), the inner dimension is unchanged. (iii) Entrywise product: if F factors through w1 and G through w2, their Hadamard product (x,y) -> F(x,y) G(x,y) factors through width w1 * w2; the inner index set is the Cartesian product of the two, with left/right factors multiplied componentwise. Widths multiply. (iv) Scaling: a constant multiple c*F factors through the same width w (absorb c into the left factor). Assembling a width bound: a threshold indicator 1[M u(x) + v(y) < T] factors through width 2 (a two-state prefix/suffix separation across the binary cut); an exponential exp(u(x)+v(y)) factors through width 1 (it splits as a product exp(u(x)) exp(v(y))); a polynomial q(u(x)+v(y)) of degree <= d factors through width d+1 (shifted Taylor). A piece like 'indicator times exponential' uses law (iii): width 2*1 = 2; 'indicator times polynomial' uses (iii): width 2*(d+1). Summing the left-tail, middle, and right-tail pieces uses law (i): the total width is the sum of the pieces' widths. Negation (ii) lets one express a difference of two indicators (a band) and scaling (iv) lets one weight the left tail by exp(-1). Because every law manipulates only the factor matrices and inner index sets, the composite width bound is obtained symbolically, never materialising the full array; the final width is a fixed linear function of the degree d (independent of the array dimensions).

question: The full target initial datum is a piecewise function: an exponential left tail for p < -1, a degree-<=2k+1 polynomial bridge for -1 <= p < 0, and an exponential right tail for p >= 0. Sample it on an integer-indexed grid and split the index as M*u(x) + v(y) across a binary cut, where v(y) < M. reference_answer: Write the sampled datum as a sum of three terms selected by threshold indicators of the integer index n(x,y) = M u(x) + v(y). Let A, B be the integer cutoffs for the thresholds p < -1 and p < 0 respectively (obtained by a ceiling of an affine expression; across the cut each threshold indicator factors through width 2). Term 1 (left tail): 1[n < A] * exp(grid), width 2 * 1 = 2 (indicator times exponential). Term 2 (middle): (1[n < B] - 1[n < A]) * q(grid), where q is the source polynomial of degree <= 2k+1. The band indicator is a difference of two width-2 indicators, so by the sum/negation laws it factors through width 2 + 2 = 4; multiplied entrywise by the polynomial of width (2k+1)+1 = 2k+2 gives width 4 * (2k+2) = 8k+8. Term 3 (right tail): (1 - 1[n < B]) * exp(-grid), the complement indicator times an exponential; the complement factors through width 2 and the exponential through width 1, so width 2 * 1 = 2. Summing the three terms adds widths: 2 + (8k+8) + 2 = 8k+12. Each threshold indicator truly separates across the binary cut because 'M u(x) + v(y) < T' reduces, using v(y) < M, to a two-row condition (u(x) < T/M, or u(x) = T/M together with v(y) < T mod M) — exactly a two-state separation. The exponential separations use exp(a+b) = exp(a) exp(b) (width 1), and the polynomial separation uses the shifted-Taylor factorization (width deg+1). The combined explicit width is a finite index set of cardinality 8k+12, so the rank of the sample array is at most 8k+12, independent of the register width and of where the cut is placed. This is a separation certificate only; it does not by itself furnish a gate compiler or a finite-precision algorithm.

question: A reader argues: 'Since the sampled Hermite amplitude array has every bipartite cut rank bounded by 8k+12, the state can be prepared by a polynomial-resource circuit; the rank bound closes the state-preparation task.' Explain why this inference is not valid as stated. Exhibit the logical gap by distinguishing what a cut-rank/factorization certificate actually provides from what a state-preparation circuit requires, and identify at least two concrete ingredients that the rank bound alone does not supply.
reference_answer: The inference conflates a structural separation certificate with a constructive compilation. What the certificate provides is: for each bipartite cut, an explicit algebraic factorization F = A B with inner dimension at most 8k+12, hence a rank bound. This is a statement about the existence and width of a low-rank decomposition of the sample matrix. What state preparation requires is strictly more: (1) an actual sequence of elementary gates (e.g. uniformly controlled rotations and CX) whose unitary's first column equals the normalized amplitude vector; (2) the real rotation angles — i.e. an isometry/QR-type completion of the low-rank factors into unitary tensors — together with a finite-precision or exact-angle model; (3) handling of normalization by the true global sample norm, which the per-cut factorization does not compute. A low rank per cut is necessary context for an MPS/TT route but not sufficient: a bounded-rank matrix of amplitudes does not come with a canonical-form gauge, an isometrization of the cores, or a bound on the arithmetic/gate cost of realising those cores. Counterexample-style gap: one can have a family of matrices all of rank 1 (the extreme low-rank case) whose entries are arbitrary efficiently-or-inefficiently describable functions; rank 1 alone says nothing about whether the single factor vectors are preparable by a short circuit or even computable to finite precision. Thus 'rank <= 8k+12 for all cuts' is compatible with both easy and hard preparation problems, so it cannot by itself close the task. The source material is explicit that the factorization certificates 'are not a gate compiler, an isometry completion, or a finite-precision algorithm,' and that a rank bound alone does not close the polynomial-resource state-preparation task; the separate normalization supplier and the explicit RY/CX circuit are additional, independent constructions.

question: A gluing principle states: if two real functions f and g are each C^k and all their derivatives through order k agree at a cut point c, then the spliced function (equal to f for x < c and g for x >= c) is C^k. A student claims the jet-matching hypothesis is unnecessary — that merely requiring f and g to be C^k and to agree in value at c (f(c) = g(c)) already gives a C^k splice. Disprove this for k = 1 with an explicit example, and explain exactly which derivative order fails and why the full jet-matching hypothesis through order k is needed for a C^k conclusion.
reference_answer: Counterexample at k = 1, cut c = 0. Take f(x) = 0 and g(x) = x. Both are C^1 (indeed C^infinity), and they agree in value at 0: f(0) = 0 = g(0). The splice is h(x) = 0 for x < 0 and h(x) = x for x >= 0, which is exactly the ReLU function (max(x,0)). Step 1 (continuity holds): h is continuous because the one value-matching condition f(0) = g(0) is satisfied; so h is C^0. Step 2 (first derivative fails): the left derivative of h at 0 is f'(0) = 0, while the right derivative is g'(0) = 1. Since 0 != 1, h is not differentiable at 0, hence not C^1. The student's weakened hypothesis (value agreement only) is therefore insufficient: it controls order 0 but leaves the order-1 jets mismatched. Step 3 (what the real principle needs): to obtain C^1 we must also require f'(0) = g'(0); more generally for C^k we need iterated-derivative agreement at every order j = 0,1,...,k. The proof of the correct principle is by induction on k: the base case uses continuity from value matching; the inductive step differentiates the splice, which is itself a splice of f' and g' (using that the one-sided derivatives coincide precisely because f'(c)=g'(c)), and then applies the hypothesis one order lower. Each induction level consumes exactly one jet-matching equation, so all k+1 equations j = 0,...,k are genuinely used. Dropping any of them breaks the chain at that order, exactly as the ReLU example breaks at order 1. Hence the jet-matching hypothesis through order k is necessary, not decorative, and value agreement alone yields only continuity.

question: The target initial datum is the piecewise function equal to exp(p) for p < -1, to the source polynomial S(p) for -1 <= p <= 0, and to exp(-p) for p > 0. Assume it is already known that S matches the required endpoint jets: all derivatives of S through order k equal those of exp at the left junction p = -1, and all derivatives of S through order k equal those of exp(-p) at the right junction p = 0. Prove that the full target is globally C^k for every natural number k, using a reusable two-piece C^k gluing theorem applied twice.
reference_answer: Represent the target as a nested double splice: first glue the polynomial piece to the right exponential at p = 0, then glue the left exponential to that result at p = -1. Step 1 (right junction, p = 0): the polynomial p -> S(p) is C^k (polynomials are C^infinity), and p -> exp(-p) is C^k (composition of exp with negation). The jet-matching hypothesis at p = 0 is given: the derivatives of S through order k equal those of exp(-p) at 0. Here one uses that the j-th derivative of exp(-p) is (-1)^j exp(-p), equal at p=0 to (-1)^j, matching the prescribed right-endpoint jet (-1)^j of S. By the two-piece C^k gluing theorem, the right splice R(p) = (S for p < 0, exp(-p) for p >= 0) is C^k. Step 2 (left junction, p = -1): now glue exp (which is C^k) to R at p = -1. The left exponential exp has j-th derivative exp, equal at p=-1 to exp(-1). On a neighborhood of p = -1 the right splice R coincides with the polynomial S (since -1 < 0, points near -1 are < 0, where R = S), so the derivatives of R at -1 equal those of S at -1, which by hypothesis equal exp(-1) through order k. Thus exp and R satisfy the jet-matching hypothesis at -1. Applying the gluing theorem again, the double splice (exp for p < -1, R otherwise) is C^k. Step 3 (identify with the target): the double splice equals the original piecewise target: for p < -1 it is exp(p); for -1 <= p < 0 it is R = S(p); at p = 0 both the <=0 and >0 conventions give value 1 (S(0) = 1 = exp(0)); for p > 0 it is exp(-p). So the target is exactly the double splice, hence C^k. Since k is arbitrary and the same argument runs for every k, the target is C^k for all k. The construction reuses a single gluing theorem twice, each application discharged by the known endpoint jets; smoothness is thus reduced entirely to the Hermite jet-matching of S.
